#9200. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9199. AI-Generated Product Photos Are Putting Off Online Shoppers, Study Finds

AI-Generated Product Photos Are Putting Off Online Shoppers, Study Finds

A majority of U.S. online shoppers say AI-generated product images make them less confident about buying a product, according to new research from e-commerce UX research organization Baymard.

The study, conducted in June 2026, surveyed 2,273 U.S. online shoppers. It found that 60% would be less confident about a purchase if they knew the product images were AI-generated.

Of those surveyed, 25% said AI-generated images would slightly reduce their confidence, while 18% said they would significantly reduce it. Another 17% said they would not feel confident enough to buy the product at all.

Just 18% said knowing an image was AI-generated would make no difference to their purchasing confidence.

The findings come as retailers increasingly turn to generative AI to produce product imagery, including lifestyle shots, virtual models, and other marketing visuals, often as a way to reduce photography costs.

Last month, PetaPixel reported that food delivery app Just Eat apologized for several inaccurate AI-generated photos on menus, including a nauseating picture of bacon and eggs floating in a soda.

Meanwhile, fashion photo studios are closing down as brands increasingly embrace AI thanks to the big savings offered by the technology.

“Shoppers don’t treat product photos as decoration. They use them to check what they’re actually going to receive: the color, the fit, the texture, the scale,” says Christian Holst, co-founder of Baymard. “An AI-generated image undermines exactly that. For one in six shoppers, it’s enough to walk away from the purchase.”

Holst adds that AI still has a place in product imagery but argues that retailers should prioritize authentic photography for core product views. AI-generated backgrounds and lifestyle scenes can be used as supporting visuals, he adds, provided brands take steps to maintain shopper trust.

Baymard recommends that retailers prioritize authentic photography for primary product images, limit AI-generated visuals to supporting content, and address potential shopper skepticism when using AI imagery.

The full findings and charts are available on Baymard’s website.

#9197. Airbnb Host Accused of Using AI-Edited Photo of Blocked Toilet to Claim $1,000 From Guest

Airbnb Host Accused of Using AI-Edited Photo of Blocked Toilet to Claim $1,000 From Guest

An Airbnb host is accused of using an AI-edited photo of an overflowing, blocked toilet to claim $1,000 from a guest.

According to a report by ABC News Australia, the dispute involves a French tourist who faced several claims from an Airbnb host, with the amounts adding up to thousands of dollars.

Two days after leaving the property, the tourist posted a one-star review following a disagreement over his checkout. The host subsequently submitted a damage claim to Airbnb requesting $1,244 ($1,755 AUD).

As evidence, the host submitted an invoice for $1,046 ($1,500 AUD) for “foreign object extraction” through Airbnb’s Resolution Center. The claim was accompanied by a photograph that appeared to show a blocked toilet with water spilling onto the bathroom floor. A second invoice showed a payment of $177 ($255 AUD) to a third party for cleaning described as “extraordinary soilage”.

The tourist questioned whether the photograph of the overflowing toilet was genuine and shared it on social media to see whether others had the same concerns. After receiving responses from other users, he decided to check the image using an AI detector, which he said indicated that the photo had been manipulated.

ABC News Australia reports that it subsequently examined the photograph of the blocked toilet using Google’s SynthID Detector. The tool found that the image had been generated or edited using Google AI.

Airbnb says it investigated the tourist’s complaint about the AI-doctored photo and rejected the host’s damage claim over the toilet. The company also reportedly refunded him almost $1,395 ($2,000 AUD) for his stays with the host and tours he had missed while spending time on the phone with Airbnb disputing the claims.

“We take reports like this seriously… the guest has been fully refunded and will not be charged,” a spokesman for Airbnb Australia and New Zealand says.

However, Airbnb did not confirm to ABC News Australia whether it would take any further action against the host following the rejected claim.

The incident follows a separate case involving a Lyft driver who was accused of using an AI-generated image to create a fake damage fee claim against a teenage passenger. A father and daughter said a recent ride ended with the driver submitting an AI-generated photograph that appeared to show a car interior covered in mess, allegedly to justify a cleaning or damage charge.

#9196. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#9195. Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government

Several items were removed from this display on 15 October Photo: Angie Matiz

Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.

On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).

The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.

Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

Empty spaces where items had been removed from the museum walls Courtesy Colombia Diversa

The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.

The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.

Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.

According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.

“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.

#9194. Photographers are Suing Uber Eats for Copyright Infringement Over Its Use of Their Food Photos

Photographers are Suing Uber Eats for Copyright Infringement Over Its Use of Their Food Photos

A group of food photographers has been given the green light to proceed with a copyright infringement lawsuit against Uber Eats.

Last year, more than 20 professional photographers sued Uber Technologies Inc., the parent company of Uber Eats, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida. They accused the company of infringing their copyrights by displaying their food photographs without permission.

The photographers say they never transferred ownership of the images or permitted Uber to use them. However, they allege that Uber copied and used the photographs on its website to advertise and promote its business and sell its products and services. They also claim Uber shared the images with its employees, contractors, customers and business partners.

In April 2026, the judge dismissed some of the photographers’ claims for vicarious and contributory copyright infringement, as well as claims relating to dozens of unregistered photographs that were not adequately alleged to be foreign works.

However, in a recent ruling, Judge Beth Bloom of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida allowed the group of professional photographers to proceed with several of their copyright infringement claims against Uber Eats over their food pictures posted on the platform. According to a report by Bloomberg Law News, Judge Bloom rejected Uber’s argument that it cannot be held liable for images uploaded to its platform by third parties.

In its request to dismiss the lawsuit, Uber argued that the photographers had failed to establish who was responsible for uploading the allegedly infringing images. However, Judge Beth Bloom ruled that they had sufficiently alleged that either Uber employees or agents, or restaurant merchants, had uploaded the photographs. She also found that Uber’s alleged practice of reviewing images before publication, and its contractual right to reject, remove, or modify them, suggested it could prevent copyright infringement.

The judge also rejected Uber’s argument that the photographers had failed to demonstrate a direct financial benefit from the alleged infringement. The photographers argued that food photographs generate more clicks and orders on Uber Eats, increasing the commissions Uber receives. The judge found these allegations sufficient, saying the photographers did not need to demonstrate that each individual copyrighted image had generated additional sales.

#9192. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

#9191. 10 Years Later, Magenta Plains Is Still Embracing the Unexpected

An anniversary exhibition spotlights the artists who’ve made the gallery one of Lower Manhattan’s most adventurous success stories.

Olivia Smith had a thriving career running Exhibition A on the Upper East Side, a company that sells original contemporary art editions, when artists Chris Dorland and David Deutsch approached her in 2015 about opening a gallery on the Lower East Side.

Smith had worked with hundreds of artists producing limited edition prints, but she had never managed a commercial gallery or negotiated with museums before. Still, she felt a kinship with Dorland and Deutsch, who found a ground-floor storefront on Allen Street and needed help programming it. First they had to agree on a name, as long as it wasn’t their own on the door.

“We wanted something expansive and open-ended,” Smith told Hyperallergic. “We felt Magenta Plains represented a place, but we didn’t know what that place was that we were building yet.”

A decade later, Magenta Plains has helped define what the Downtown contemporary art scene can offer the world. The gallery, which outgrew its original location and currently occupies a 4,500-square-foot space at 149 Canal Street, has featured groundbreaking technology-influenced installations, sculptures, and paintings, selections of which are on display in its 10 Year Anniversary show, up through October 31.

#9190. Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum

The Tsaritsyno palace in Moscow Photo courtesy the office of the mayor of Moscow, via Wikimedia Commons

Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.

On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.

The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.

In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”

The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.

The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.

The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.

Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

As the Moscow institution is temporarily closed and its director, Roman Romanov, is dismissed, fears grow that Russia’s past is being glossed over

#9189. The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party

From “Las Dos Fridas” to a walking Eva Hesse sculpture, Hyperallergic members, readers, friends, and artists brought the spirit of the season to our second annual costume contest.

A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... That’s a Hyperallergic Halloween, baby!

On Wednesday evening, October 28, almost 200 of our members, readers, artists, supporters, and their enthusiastic friends rolled into Oberon in Brooklyn for our annual art costume party. Winners in several categories ranging from “Best in Show” to “Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida” brought out the art-history nerd within them, materializing into both immediately recognizable icons — Roy Lichtenstein's “Drowning Girls” and Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” — and admirably obscure references (oh, she was an Eva Hesse rope sculpture?!).

We’re so grateful to our absurdly smart, creative, and crafty community for their commitment to the bit. And a big shout-out to Zac Thompson for their incredible photographs, which will help us relive the night for many moons, or at least as we wait impatiently for next year ... 🌝

Best in Show winners Emilio Rojas and Chico Raro as Pedro Lemebel and Francisco Casa Silva of Las Yeguas del Apocalipsis’s “Las Dos Fridas” (1989). No bribing was necessary to convince the panel.

Zoë Lescaze and Michael Rossi made every part of their costumes from scratch — yes, including the chair — to dress as lesser-known characters from Francisco Goya's Los caprichos (1797–98) series. The couple was among the winners of the "Most Esoteric" award, naturally.

Richard Prince's "Wayward Nurse" (2005), part of the artist's series critiquing the sexualization of nurses on pulp-fiction book covers, would not fly in the Sunshine State in 2026!

Curators and staff from the Heckscher Museum of Art in Huntington, New York, recreated a painting from the institution's own collection: George Grosz's antifascist "Eclipse of the Sun" (1926).

Melissa Brown and Marie Lorenz won over the crowd as none other than the infamously botched “Ecce Homo” aka “Beast Jesus” and its author, restorer Cecilia Giménez Zueco!

Hyperallergic Co-founders Veken Gueyikian and Hrag Vartanian with one of this year's costume contest judges, Nicholas D. Lowry, president of Swann Auction Galleries. Veken is Kazimir Malevich’s “Black Square” (1915), and Vartanian is a 17th-century Dutch still life painting — check out the skull! (Memento mori, very Halloween-coded.)

Lowry as a fashionable pumpkin in plaid.

Hyperallergic Staff Writer Anna Lee as Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (c. 1665) — an art-history classic, made otherworldly by photographer Zac Thompson’s expert double exposure.

These guests brought Museo del Prado right to your doorstep as a rather gory version of Francisco Goya's “Saturn Devouring His Son” (1820–23). Body horror!

Artist Coco Fusco donned one of the fabulous works in Marisol's wearable wooden sculpture "Three Women with Umbrella" (1965–66). Who says Pop art is dead?

If we had a “Cutest” category this year, this pawesome group would have taken the gold! Left to right: Will Swanson, Dwai, Cosette Patterson, Lauren Blaser, Shelby Roller, Sophia Tedesco, and Daniela Alonso as Cassius Marcellus Coolidge’s “A Friend in Need” (1903).

Emily Dotsikas of Alma Communications as Roy Lichtenstein’s “Drawing Girl” (1963). Brad, who?

Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara addresses the crowd after a very competitive contest. Just don't ask him what his costume is!

Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Rest Energy” (1980). There’s nothing scarier than a multi-year situationship, except maybe literally putting your heart in the hands of your lover.

Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar went as Snoopy for the fourth year in a row, a costume she calls her “magnum opus.”

“I made this Snoopy costume with stuff that I already had at home — the ears, spot, and tail were from an old black tee; I painted an old beauty blender black and used it as Snoopy's nose,” Nayyar shared. “My love of this cartoon beagle is well-known and documented. I'm already a crazy dog lady, but there's something about Snoopy's cheeky attitude and ridiculous antics that flips the script on the ‘man's best friend’ marker, which I find really liberating and inspirational.”

Artist agent Anna Staub (left) and curator and gallerist Yuna Cabon of Third Born (right) joined forces, quite literally, to embody Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Relation in Time” (1977).

What still life is complete without its peckish butterfly? Houry Geudelekian and Hyperallergic Co-founder and Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian make a perfect pair.

Us: “What are you?”Artist Danielle De Jesus: “I'm a broke MFA student!”

Just brilliant, down to the Whitney Museum artist lifetime pass!

Hyperallergic contributors Julie Schneider (middle) as a Keith Haring subway drawing and Daniela Mayer (far right) as an AI girlfriend, with Felix Moody as water and Brian Henderson as Candy Warhol (not pictured: candy corn costume).

Artists Jesse Lambert as Ray Johnson and Linda Ganjian as Eva Hesse's rope sculpture "No title" (1970). Is this what they mean by a two-person show?

#9188. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

#9187. To Live Is to Believe

Remembering Ursula von Rydingsvard, an Epstein survivor’s message for MoMA, interviews with Paul Pfeiffer and Layli Long Soldier, and the best costumes of our artsy Halloween party.

On a fair afternoon in Queens, New York, a woman in a red dress crosses the street in front of me with an actual axe under her arm. Her face is stern, her step fast, and you can tell from the blood on her axe that she wasn’t using it to chop wood. A police siren wails in the distance, but that doesn’t seem to bother her.

I reach to lock the car and then remember it’s Halloween.

At a warm and lovely dinner at Cabinet Magazine, founder and editor-in-chief Sina Najafi shows us a photograph of tightrope walker Margret Zimmermann balancing on a high wire above the bombed-out ruins of the Haymarket in Cologne, Germany, in 1946. She looks her finest in her red lipstick, but a treacherous wind is blowing in her hair as a crowd watches from far below.

Outside, Brooklyn seems to be getting richer and poorer at the same time. A man wearing a bejeweled crown asks me for money. In this city, performance artists are beggars and beggars are performance artists.

At Hyperallergic’s art-themed Halloween party, dozens of guests show up with impressive costumes and really commit to the act. Claire Valdez, an artist and organizer who’s running for Congress, drops by and serves as a judge in our art costume contest. I don’t have a costume, but I perform all night.

“To live is to believe,” Marcel Duchamp says in a video on my phone screen. A little girl dressed as Lady Liberty crosses the street with her mother, a torch in her hand. She keeps the torch held high as they walk off, and that makes me smile.

A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... That’s a Hyperallergic Halloween, baby! #9185. Kohei Yamada: MY SCREEN TESTS @ Gr Gallery, New York (UPDATED with Installation Imagery)

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent

longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. New York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against New York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

The opening reception will take place on Friday, May 15 from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. The artist will participate in the opening reception.

#9184. Applications are Open for the Core Residency Program at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston

Join a cohort of artists and writers committed to developing a sustainable practice. Applications for the 2027–29 Core term are due January 8, 2027.

The Core Residency Program at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston (MFAH) awards residencies to exceptional, highly motivated emerging artists and critical writers committed to developing a sustainable practice. The residency term is from September 2027 to July 2029.

Fellows are provided with a private studio space and regular studio visits from artists and curators. They also receive free and discounted classes at the MFAH’s Glassell School of Art and may request access to fabrication studios, including those for painting, printmaking, digital and film photography, sculpture, jewelry, and ceramics.

Additionally, fellows have access to the MFAH and its galleries and collections; its two house museums for American and Europeans decorative arts; borrowing privileges at the Hirsch Library of the MFAH and the Fondren Library at Rice University.

Applications for the 2027–29 Core term are due January 8, 2027. For instructions and more information, visit mfah.org/core.

Elmwood's Kyle Whybrow discusses the increasing hunger for tactile and intentional design.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As part of its 40th anniversary, Dolmio has revived its iconic puppet family. After a 10-year hiatus, the reintroduction of these familiar faces is both a return to tactile branding and a welcome nostalgia trip for fans.

Starring in some of the best adverts of the 2000s, the Dolmio family carries quite the legacy for the brand. In a world of social-first branding and AI slop advertising, Dolmio's return to form is an ingenious response to audiences that are growing increasingly hungry for human-led design.

To understand more about the Dolmio family's grand return, I caught up with Kyle Whybrow, ECD at Elmwood London, to understand the value of nostalgia and the art of reviving brand heritage.

The Dolmio brand and family were both born in Australia. Dolmio started life as a single bolognese sauce in a glass jar, and its success saw it grow into an established brand reaching wider markets, including the UK. Papa and Mama were originally cast as actors, then reimagined as handcrafted puppet characters in 2003, with the wider family joining them: Sophia, Carlo, Nina and Nico.

The idea behind them was simple and very human: the noisy, loving chaos of a family sitting down to eat together. In the UK, ‘When’s your Dolmio Day?’ turned a jar of sauce into a family ritual. They weren’t mascots bolted onto a product. They were the brand’s personality, given a face.

The puppets have grown up with the families watching them. The originals were definitely of their time, but our job wasn’t to replace them. It was to bring them into a modern family home, fit for today’s audience.

We gave each character clear principles, behaviours and visual codes, so each one has a distinct, contemporary personality. Then we built them into Dolmio’s wider identity, the red dot system, with real intent, so the family feels native to the brand’s graphic language rather than placed on top of it.

That system is consistent but flexible. One character can pop up inside the red dot, or the whole family can take the stage, whether that’s talking about the jar or sharing the moment over a bowl of pasta or a lasagne. That flexibility is what lets them stay culturally aware and show up in the moments that matter today. In the past they lived in a 30-second spot. Now they move between culture, content and commerce.

With respect, and a fine-tuned difference. We started by asking what made each character unmistakable, then amplified those details rather than diluting them. The silhouettes, the expressions and the family dynamic all stayed. Then we went deep on craft.

Every detail was considered and balanced: the subtle nuances in their features that feel familiar yet new, the clothing, the choice of material, the texture of their skin and hair, right down to the micro facial expressions and the wrinkles under the eyes. We took learnings from the great puppet and animation houses, because those tiny movements are what make a character feel alive and let people connect with them.

It was all about respecting where they came from while making them feel right for a modern audience. The red dot and the family make each other stronger: one gives instant recognition, the other gives people something to love. Fresh doesn’t have to mean new. Sometimes it just means sharper.

Nostalgia is a double-edged sword. Change too little, and you’re running a tribute act. Change too much, and you break the bond people have with these characters.

The other challenge was range and versatility across paid, shared, earned and owned. The same family had to deliver an emotional moment on TV, a shareable piece of culturally relevant content on social, and a clear reason to buy at the shelf. That meant building a proper system of rules, not one-off executions. Working closely with T&P was crucial here, so the family showed up consistently, whatever the channel or moment in the year.

Honestly, the invisible work. Anyone can bring back a much-loved character for a nostalgic moment. Building the principles, behaviours and codes that let a whole family perform consistently across every touchpoint is much harder.

I’m proud that each character feels truly distinct, yet they all clearly belong to Dolmio. And I love that they work as ambassadors as well as entertainers: they inspire people on social and still help convert them at the shelf. That’s design doing a commercial job as well as an emotional one.

I think audiences are hungry for craft and intent, and they can tell when it’s missing. The original Dolmio family were handmade puppets, and that tactile quality is a big part of why people love them.

You can’t buy decades of memory, but if you have it, it’s one of the most powerful distinctive assets a brand can own.

For the 40th, the family was rebuilt digitally, so we held every frame to the standard of the handmade originals. That’s why I don’t see it as analogue versus technology. Unreal Engine, motion capture, or the Puppetiser in Australia that lets families ‘puppetise’ themselves are brilliant when they serve the idea. Slop happens when the tool becomes the idea.

Because it’s earned. You can’t buy decades of memory, but if you have it, it’s one of the most powerful distinctive assets a brand can own. Nostalgia gives you instant recognition and connection, and it gives you permission to be playful. The trap is treating it as a rerun. Nostalgia works hardest when it bridges generations: parents who grew up with the Dolmio family get a smile of recognition, and their kids meet the characters for the first time and find them relevant now. It travels across markets too, because a family sitting down to eat needs no translation. That’s when nostalgia stops looking backwards and starts building the future.

#9182. Barbara Takenaga’s ‘Awestruck’

At Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, 40 paintings invite viewers into an exhibition where scale, pattern, and perception are explored and celebrated.

On view at Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art in Kansas City through April 11, 2027, Barbara Takenaga: Awestruck presents the artist’s first comprehensive survey in nearly a decade. Bringing together 40 works spanning her career since the early 2000s, the exhibition reveals the many approaches to abstraction that have shaped Takenaga’s practice. The exhibition is organized by Jessica May, Ph.D., Executive Director, Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, and Tae Edell, Independent Curator.

The exhibition examines Barbara Takenaga’s intricate compositions through four thematic sections: an emphasis on process, a masterful confusion of scale, an embrace of illusion, and reverent nods to art history. Together, these strategies work to upend the viewer’s expectations, engaging imagination and stoking curiosity for more.

Featuring works from institutional and private collections across the nation, this exhibition includes paintings up to her most recent, revealing Takenaga’s continued push to further her approach across increasingly expanding canvases, opening new paths within her ongoing exploration of abstraction.

#9181. Comment | There is cautious optimism surrounding the contemporary art market—but will it last?

Yes, no or neutral: the spectrum of art market confidence is captured by ArtTactic’s report Gesrey/Adobe Stock

There is an irony to trying to gauge the health of the art market, as so many in the industry are doing now, with New York’s marquee auctions, the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi and the latest Art Collaboration Kyoto ahead this month. On the one hand, the trade is endlessly driven by emotion. On the other, few broad-based, rigorous read-outs can be found of how the participants actually feel about the state of play.

But one exception that proves this rule was published recently: the September edition of ArtTactic’s report on confidence in the contemporary art market. It adds quantitative heft to the sentiment that has emerged from more and more reporting since the spring. Although the market has not caught fire yet, the findings indicate that significant segments of it have certainly thawed. More importantly, a cross-section of experts with skin in the game expect the (modestly) good times to continue for the foreseeable future.

So what is the Contemporary Art Market Confidence Report? Twice a year, the study asks a cross-section of collectors, advisers, auction house professionals and other market participants whether they feel positive, negative or neutral about aspects of the art trade and the wider economy in the US and Europe. ArtTactic then converts the ratings into a single score, from zero (essentially, no confidence) to 100 (essentially, absolute confidence), for each question, offering a quantified, collective evaluation.

The main takeaway is encouraging but measured. The overall confidence indicator rose from 43 (slightly pessimistic) in March 2026 to 56 (slightly optimistic) in September. It marks only the third time the rating has reached positive territory in more than four years.

However, both previous moments of optimism were short-lived. After hitting a rowdy 75 in February 2022, the rating dropped to 42 that July. And the January 2025 score of 54 plunged to a frightening 30 six months later.

Anders Petterson, the founder and chief executive of ArtTactic, thinks the current bout of positivity is more durable than the last one. In January 2025, he points out, 39% of the survey respondents expected Donald Trump’s return to the White House to produce economic policies that would boost the art market. “Instead, he introduced tariffs and a significant amount of uncertainty, which pulled down confidence for the July 2025 reading,” Petterson says. The difference now is that the “confidence seems to be grounded in a real recovery in sales, rather than just a belief”.

Still, the experts polled by ArtTactic are nearly as wary as they are optimistic. Asked whether sales would rise, fall or stay flat over the six months to come, 60% chose the last of these options.

That may not sound great, but it isn’t bad. Remember, a confidence indicator of 56 means most of the respondents believe things are good right now, even if only just. In this context, Petterson says that a flat outlook for the next half year “suggests stability rather than deterioration”.

Some parts of the market appear steadier than others, however. Confidence in the auction market—up to 78 from 69 in March, spurred on by results at the top end­—far surpassed confidence in the primary market, which nudged up to 51 from 45. Although this is good news for the trade at large, the visibility of strong hammer results tends not to boost all sellers equally.

“Most of the recovery at auction is still concentrated in the above $1m segment, which is likely to benefit galleries/artists operating at the top end,” Petterson says. “What is less clear is whether, and how quickly, that confidence will make its way down to lower-price-point galleries and artists.”

Galleries may need to do more to help themselves. On the eve of Frieze week, the American adviser Adam Green said he has seen “a noticeable shift” among many of his clients. Offputtingly high and persistent prices for new works have pushed several collectors who often used to buy from primary market dealers toward auction houses and private resellers, both of which “can provide a better opportunity to acquire works closer to their true fair market value”.

Although Green believes market recovery is “broadening to some degree”, he also suspects its full reach will take until the end of the year to become clear. If you wanted to translate the ArtTactic report data into one simple sentiment, it would be hard to do it more efficiently than in that sentence. Now we know this sentiment really is shared by more than just a few industry figures that we journalists happened to ask for comment.

The divide between primary and secondary markets blur as sales skew in favour of a few recognised, bankable artists

While ancient art and ceramics remain popular, Contemporary Chinese art is taking off at home, and buyers outside the mainland are slowly looking toward Western art

#9178. Ana Mendieta's Lasting Imprint on Art

A major survey at Tate Modern asks us to take notice of the earth, the power of the female body, and the artist’s remarkable practice.

LONDON — Barely there but deftly constructed, Ana Mendieta’s Siluetas could be anywhere. Some are almost invisible in her documentary photographs. In one from 1979, a human form is impressed into the mud among similar natural shapes on a dried-out riverbank. In another from 1978, a few shimmering leaves, flowers, and branches sketch out the ghost of a woman against a dark tree trunk. Ana Mendieta, a major survey exhibition at Tate Modern, however, asks us to take notice: of the earth, the power of the female body, and the artist’s remarkable practice.

The exhibition eschews a chronological approach, opting to organize works according to their physical and metaphorical places, such as The Grove, The School, or The Sacred Grounds. This effectively points visitors towards the essential site-specificity of Mendieta’s practice; individual works are made in dialogue with particular locations of personal, ecological, or spiritual significance. More broadly, as the wall text explains, Mendieta described her practice as an “attempt to return to the maternal source,” in response to being “cast from the womb (Nature)” through her exile from Cuba as a child.

The exhibition opens with “The Cave,” featuring late works from the 1980s, including her very last video piece “Ochún” (1981) and a selection of her “rupestrian” sculptures inspired by prehistoric rock art. Whereas her more famous Silueta series generally features an imprint or silhouette of Mendieta’s own body, these lesser-known later works are more open-ended in style. Here, female forms are borrowed not from the artist’s anatomy but from the natural forms of rocks and prehistoric representations of goddesses.

Christopher Glass shares his industry insight for the next generation of creatives.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a creative industry grappling with the increasing influence of AI, it can be disheartening for a newcomer. It seems every day we're met with news of job layoffs and new 'time-saving' tools that skimp on human creativity, but industry vet Christopher Glass is here to settle your woes.

With over 20 years in the filmmaking industry, Christopher has seen a huge evolution (check out our previous interview for more). As a production designer leveraging the power of practical effects, he argues that there's still space for tactile design in the film world – all it takes is a bit of courage and open-mindedness.

Christopher Glass is an Art Director Guild (ADG) Award-winning and Gold Cannes Lion-winning Production Designer whose work spans feature films, television, and commercials. Known for creating visually ambitious, emotionally resonant worlds - he has collaborated with some of the most influential directors working in film and advertising today.

I wish people knew what production designers do. Most people don’t. A lot of my own family don’t understand what I do for a living. It’s easy to say we are responsible for the look of everything in a film except the costumes, cinematography and the off-camera lighting, but even that sounds ambiguous, and it really doesn’t explain all of the things production designers do day to day. A lot of producers and even some directors don’t know either. The good ones do!

Actors always respond better to real sets, people and FX. It’s simple. They have incredible imaginations; however, nothing beats having something there to interact with.

AI is the antithesis of feelings. It is a removal of humanity. It is something we, as designers, “feel” forced and obligated to use due to economics and survival. AI can do some amazing technical things.

For instance, there is no reason to ever have green screens again or LED volumes. I feel bad for those who invested heavily in LED walls. Rig removal can be done instantaneously. Set extensions will soon be a snap. That’s technically useful and economically enticing. It can also be used as a fast way to make references and communicate visual intentions.

Many people will lose work if they don’t adapt to this monster being forced on us without our choice. At the end of the day, humans are more capable of coming up with novel ideas. We have lives, memories, true emotions and experiences that haven’t ever been posted onto a forum or social media platform for the AI vacuum machines to suck up and regurgitate with a prompt.

Don’t let the tech weenies make you think we will become extinct as designers and artists. Don’t let them decide. Use their tools against them. And also keep an open mind. Find like-minded people to collaborate with. Film is a collaborative medium, and being able to admit when you don’t know something is as important as knowing something.

Be humble, yet courageous and confident at the same time. Go to museums and study history. Dream. Also, learn budgeting! It has taken me a while to get to that point.

#9176. How Former Theater Kid James Talarico Stands Up for the Arts in Texas

As Republicans exert an ever-tightening grip on creative freedom in the state, the Democratic Senate hopeful stands out for his track record on arts funding.

Every United States election season, a few candidates capture national attention. This year, one of those names is Democrat James Talarico, who is running for Senate against Republican Ken Paxton. A former theater kid turned language arts teacher now serving his fourth term in the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico would become the first Democrat elected US Senator since the 1980s if he wins.

Talarico has largely built his platform tackling education, a tough battle in a state that has seen eight school district takeovers since 2020. Among the bills he has co-authored is one that focuses on fine arts funding for public schools. Over the past years, the Texas arts scene has sat at the nexus between funding cuts and censorship.

First brought up in 2023 and subsequently reintroduced in 2025, the bill would have been the first of its kind in Texas, had it passed.

“This means hundreds of millions of dollars in new funding for music, dance, art, and theater programs! It’s a game changer,” Talarico, who has an endorsement from the Actors’ Equity Association, wrote on X in 2023. Hyperallergic has contacted Talarico’s campaign for comment.

Before earning his degrees in government and education, Talarico participated in his high school’s theater program, playing two leading roles: Danny Zuko in Grease and Aslan in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

“Research shows fine arts programs improve student achievement, graduation rates, and mental health,” Talarico continued in his post. “I know it did for me when I was growing up.”

Austin-based artist Jean-Pierre Verdijo told Hyperallergic that he’s intrigued by Talarico’s overall message, which he views as focused on fair governance as opposed to fighting another party.

#9175. French Galleries Accuse Art Basel Paris of "Disrespect, Even Contempt"

A group representing over a quarter of the exhibitors released a letter demanding compensation following the fair's abrupt closure.

Five days after Art Basel Paris announced it would prematurely terminate its 2026 edition on October 23, the Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA), an industry group representing over a quarter of the fair's exhibitors, issued a letter demanding fair compensation and accusing event organizers of poor communication and mistreatment.

In the letter addressed to the new director of Art Basel Paris, Karim Crippa, the association demanded “concrete proposals for compensating exhibitors," stated that the galleries were never consulted about the event's early closure, and accused organizers of "disrespect, even contempt," according to Monopol. Along with CPGA President and Mon Charpentier gallery co-founder Philippe Charpentier, 14 members of the board signed the letter in support. The day after the association issued the letter, Crippa reportedly wrote to exhibitors promising a "concrete update in the coming days."

On October 22, event organizers for Art Basel Paris emailed exhibitors announcing that "in light of potential demonstrations across Paris this weekend and in the interest of safeguarding our visitors," the fair would close two days ahead of its planned October 25 end date. Following a temporary lockdown during installation at the Grand Palais on October 17, organizers proceeded with the original program before agreeing to end the fair early, citing the ongoing rallies over France’s failing education system and public services that have swept across the nation since mid-September.

Mother Design’s Jo Tulej discusses the team’s unconventional approach to design.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The world of spiritualism is, by nature, an intangible force that defies definition, so what happens when a psychic services platform reaches out to you looking for a new brand identity? For the team at Mother Design, it was far from a linear process, with séances, chakra readings and intuitive creativity that challenge the confines of traditional design.

The best rebrands have the power to breathe new life into a brand, and Purple Garden's serenely beautiful new identity is no different. Born of spontaneity and experimentation, this unique rebrand is proof that the unconventional can result in something truly divine.

With Mother Design’s Wild Card initiative in mind, the team worked with a Purple Garden holistic practitioner to encourage experimentation with unfamiliar disciplines. Creating instinctively with paper and charcoal, the designers sought to bypass conscious thought, with the resulting forms, textures and feelings becoming a creative foundation for the identity.

"Transferring something as intangible as psychic power into a brand identity was a chunky challenge that we wanted to get right," explains Jo Tulej, creative director at Mother Design. "It had to begin with the audience. Purple Garden is aimed at people who have had spiritual readings and practices, and the business objective was to cement the brand’s place as the leader in the category. Therefore, we had to create something visual and verbal that would feel familiar and resonate with these ‘seasoned seekers’, but in a fresh way, that would communicate Purple Garden’s elevated offering.

In order for us to tap into that, we knew we had to experience it ourselves to understand and make something that felt authentic. Some of the Mother Design team had experience with spirituality; others didn’t, so we enlisted the help of a holistic practitioner from the platform to guide us through a chakra reading and automatic drawing and writing workshop. A brand audit with a twist, you might say!"

"The word séance comes from the words sitting or session. We were inspired by Hilma af Klint and The Five, a group of women who would come together and enter trance states to bypass conscious thought and draw and write freely. They believed they were connecting with a higher consciousness and receiving messages which translated into the marks they were making. Af Klint is a pioneer of Western abstract art, and her work predates the likes of Kandinsky and Mondrian.

We wanted to immerse ourselves in spirituality and see if that could be baked into a design process in order to create great work. The chakra reading and automatic drawing/writing took place as a group workshop in which the whole team participated. We then came back a few days later and sat alongside the drawings and writing and discussed what we were seeing and noticing. To have had this experience with an advisor from Purple Garden was an invaluable way to gain insight as well as an invigorating creative process," Jo continues.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Life and vitality breathe throughout the design, manifesting in the wordmark's combination of elegant serifs and curved junctures that appear to grow outwards. Paired with a digital-first, crystal-like glyph, the design positions Purple Garden as a source for "grounded guidance", while Literatura Present and ABC Social typefaces balance feelings of whimsy with practical legibility.

Spiritual energy emanates from the brand's diverse imagery, capturing images of "charged objects" to represent services like dream analysis and psychic readings. With "solarised glows and flame-like ripples", each image represents the energy exchange between practitioner and customer. Naturally, the colour scheme features a variety of rich purples associated with intuition and higher consciousness.

"This year we’ve been so lucky to rebrand not one but two psychic services platforms (Keen and Purple Garden)," Jo says. "What has surprised me is how different the two product/brands now feel, and how divergently we’ve been able to explore and push their identities. Again, this all comes down to getting under the skin of the audiences and aims of the business in order to sharpen the creative ideas and design expression.

I was struck by how the initial séance experiment gave us a totally different way of starting a branding project.

For the Purple Garden process specifically, I was struck by how the initial séance experiment gave us a totally different way of starting a branding project. It was slow, unclear and required a lot of trust and to a certain extent, vulnerability, from our team. By protecting this time, and removing a traditional ‘KPI’ from the output, I believe it gave our client a much richer, robust output, sensitive to the category and its audience.

So often in the branding process we have less time that we’d like, and the more intangible ideas can get pushed to the side, but at Mother Design we always try to protect this ‘wild card’ time and encourage our brilliant team to experiment."

"One challenge we faced was how to create a world that feels of the spiritual category and familiar to its fans, but also fresh and exciting, avoiding the clichés whilst drawing on symbolism that would feel universal. So we did use the category (and namesake) purple, of course, but built out a much earthier, richer palette of 7 hues to stand out against the category’s usual flatter tone. We also used pictures of nature, but they appear transformed through these solarised glows, so they have a new, magical quality to them.

Similarly, in messaging we had to find the right balance of engaging customers to take action without falling into the category tropes of urgency and pressure, ie. Book fast. Get answers. Act now. Instead, we created a voice based around a duality: Active Contemplation, that can meet you where you are and either guide you forward or slow down for more reflective moments," Jo explains.

"There’s a ton of detail and craft that went into everything, for example, creating a wordmark with ligatures that feel as though they’re sprouting, and the organic, interconnecting letter placement. The team spent a long time experimenting with lots of different processes and tools till they found a visual style for the charged objects that felt right for depicting spiritual experiences. I’m really proud of all those details that emerge the more you engage with the identity and the impact it has.

I’m also proud of the way each part of the identity, from the charged objects, to the living type, to the guiding voice, all work together to express the Living Practice idea and sense of continual growth; so it really feels like a world as opposed to disparate elements," Jo concludes.
