#9173. “The Man I Love” Wants Us to Do More Than Mourn

Ira Sachs resists the attention economy, using objects and people to tell a moving story of 1980s New York amid the HIV/AIDS crisis.

In a scene that might be this century’s most faithful depiction of 1980s bohemian New York, a ragtag ensemble crowds around a cluttered dining room table. A mishmash of stemware gleams below the revelers, each importuned to perform a few bars of a song. One self-consciously croons “Someone’s in the Kitchen with Dinah,” another vibratos a Jehovah’s Witness spiritual, while yet another gamely stumbles through the verses of “How Are Things in Glocca Morra?” from Finian’s Rainbow (1968). As gloriously languid as it is insistently idiosyncratic, the tableau readily summons nostalgia for those who remember and those who do not alike. There are no screens; there are no smartphones. There are instead people singing — shyly, joyfully — as though sharing the secret to the universe.

And they are singing, knowing full well that some in the room might not last the year.

A cinematic elegy that urges you to live, Ira Sachs’s The Man I Love is an AIDS movie that isn’t — a movie set in the thick of the pandemic that not only never mentions the illness by name, but entirely dodges the genre’s clichés: no lesion reveal, no tidy redemption, no funeral filled with festive friends. Instead, the film enjoins us to embrace the vitality of the era so as to more potently suffer its imminent loss.

The Man I Love follows “theatre artist” Jimmy George (Rami Malek), a veteran of a downtown performance troupe, as he co-writes a new production and becomes enamored of a young Englishman named Vincent (Luther Ford) who moves into the downstairs unit of their weathered prewar building. Jimmy’s partner Dennis (Tom Sturridge) tolerates the burgeoning affair, but is duly irked by Vincent’s awkward attempts to ingratiate himself into their extensive queer network.

#9172. Italy set to create restitution panel for Nazi-looted art

Edouard Manet’s Portrait de M. Arnaud à cheval (1875) was sold in 1935 by the family of painter Max Liebermann, and is now in Milan’s Galleria d’Arte Moderna Galleria d’arte moderna di Milano

Italy’s parliament is considering legislation that would, for the first time, establish a formal process for restituting art and cultural property seized by the Nazis and Italian authorities from victims of racial persecution during the Holocaust era.

Introduced by a lawmaker from Brothers of Italy, the party led by the country’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni, the proposal has been hailed by as “an act of civilisation” by representatives of heirs of those whose property was stolen, and would bring Italy in line with Germany, Austria, France, the Netherlands, the UK and Switzerland, the latest European country to establish its own restitution mechanisms.

The bill grants the government powers to establish a five-member committee to examine the provenance of works that were confiscated, looted or sold under duress as a result of racial persecution between 1933 and 1945. The committee would assess individual cases and issue decisions on restitution to the original owners, their heirs or—if no living heirs are identified—the broader Jewish community in Italy.

If enacted, the bill, which is currently being examined by the lower house’s culture committee, would give the government six months to establish the restitution system.

“Introducing this bill does not merely mean finally bringing Italy into line with the highest international standards... but means, first and foremost, fulfilling a historic duty,” Federico Mollicone, a key Meloni ally who introduced the bill in March, tells The Art Newspaper.

“We are not merely talking about property claims, but about restoring human dignity, memory and the fundamental principles of our constitution,” says Mollicone, who is the president of the culture commission in Italy’s lower house of parliament.

State-sponsored looting, confiscation and forced sale of Jewish-owned art and cultural heritage became increasingly commonplace following the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini’s 1938 introduction of racial laws that prohibited Jewish books, excluded Jews from public office and introduced limits on Jewish property ownership. The dispossessions increased from 1943, when Italian and occupying German Nazi forces began arresting and deporting Jews to concentration camps.

Some of the seized works subsequently entered the collections of Italian museums, where four publicly known disputed works are currently displayed, according to Katharina Hüls-Valenti, an expert in provenance research at Parma University. They include Edouard Manet’s Portrait de M. Arnaud à cheval (1875), which Hüls-Valenti says was sold under duress in 1935 by its owners, the family of German painter Max Liebermann, and donated to the Galleria d’Arte Moderna in Milan in 1958. Hüls-Valenti says that Liebermann’s heirs had sought restitution but had encountered resistance from the museum.

Asked to respond to those allegations, Paola Zatti, a curator at the Galleria d’Arte Moderna, said in a statement to The Art Newspaper: “The painting was sold by Liebermann’s wife in 1935 (incidentally, to a Jewish antiques dealer), but there is no evidence that she was forced to do so.”

Zatti added that, in accord with a lawyer representing Liebermann’s heirs in Germany, the museum had agreed to display a label explaining the work’s ownership history. The text, Zatti said, “clearly highlights the tragic moment when the work was sold by its Jewish owners” and helps visitors appreciate the “circumstances under which [the work] left Germany”.

Another painting, Cristo portacroce (around 1508-09) by Girolamo da Romano, was requisitioned by France’s pro-Nazi Vichy government in 1941 from the family of Federico Gentili di Giuseppe, an Italian Jewish businessman and art collector living in Paris. It was auctioned to a private collector and then bought by Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera museum in 1998. Following a request by the heirs, US authorities seized the work while it was on loan to a Florida museum in 2011.

The real number of Holocaust-era seizures currently held by museums, Hüls-Valenti suggests, could be closer to dozens. “We really don’t know for sure,” she says. “Better research is required.”

Italy endorsed the 1998 Washington Principles, which established guidelines for the restitution of Nazi-looted art. A 2001 enquiry led by Tina Anselmi, a former Italian government minister, found evidence of systematic expropriation from Jews. It found evidence of 7,847 seizure warrants issued up to April 1945 for property including houses and land, businesses, bank deposits, insurance policies, jewellery, paintings and furniture.

Despite the report’s findings, Italy, a global leader in securing the restitution of its own national heritage, has been slower than other European countries to seek justice for dispossessed Jews. France created a commission for restitutions and compensation in 1999. The UK established the Spoliation Advisory Panel in 2000 to evaluate claims to works held by British national institutions.

“Italy is obviously a central country in the world of art... and yet on this issue of the Holocaust restitution it had barely scratched the surface in addressing it,” says Gideon Taylor, the president of World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO).

Experts point to various reasons for the delay in Italy’s response, including a national reluctance to confront the country’s fascist past, insufficient political will to prioritise the restitution of Jewish-owned cultural heritage, and a lack of transparency about provenance in museums. They say poor cataloguing has contributed to an assumption that few works would be affected by a law.

Complicating matters, Italian law recognises works held in Italian museums as inalienable parts of the national heritage. The bill addresses this hurdle by indicating that the final restitution decision would automatically remove the work from the public domain. Further, restituted works would no longer be subject to the protections of Italy’s heritage code, meaning they could permanently leave the country. The bill also indicates that existing statutes of limitations would not prevent restitutions.

The commission would accept claims from legitimate owners, their descendants or heirs, and the Union of Italian Jewish Communities (UCEI) or individual Jewish communities. It would include a member nominated by Italy’s art police and have to rule within 180 days of a claim. The bill is intended to help heirs seeking restitution from both public and private collections.

Italy’s parliament adopted the bill following the submission of a report evaluating the country’s restitutions record commissioned by the WJRO and written by the lawyer Lorenzo Casini, a former chief of staff at the culture ministry who now heads a public research institution in Lucca. It was written with the support of six leading experts, including Hüls-Valenti, the Parma professor.

“Museums don’t necessarily hide their works, but there isn’t full understanding of just how important transparency is and how helpful it would be for all these works to come to light,” Casini says. “Besides addressing the tragic wounds left by looting and filling the legislative gap in Italy, the law is specifically designed to bring those artworks to light.”

Speaking to parliament’s culture commission in June, Casini praised the bill but suggested areas for improvement, proposing widening the commission’s remit from art to other cultural heritage—including manuscripts, books, archives and ceremonial objects—and advising that the commission and researchers would require additional funds to carry out their work.

“The next step could hopefully be to seek funding once the law has been passed,” Casini tells The Art Newspaper.

Federico Mollicone says lawmakers will “ensure” the culture ministry’s upcoming funding plans include “adequate resources to support research projects on provenance, the digitisation of archives, and the training of dedicated experts”. He highlights culture minister Alessandro Giuli’s “strong commitment to this issue”.

He also predicts the bill will have a smooth passage into law, noting that there is “wide political consensus” on redressing injustices from racial persecution. Brothers of Italy has roots in the post-fascist parties that rose from the ashes of the Second World War.

“Our goal is to complete the parliamentary review and pass the bill in the coming months,” Mollicone says. “We want to bring this historic reform to a successful conclusion within this legislative session.” A general election is due to take place before the end of next year, with analysts suggesting it may be brought forward to the spring.

Paolo Gnignati, UCEI’s head of legal affairs, says the bill’s arrival in parliament is significant. “The regulations on restitution are something that can be meaningful to specific individuals because they have financial and personal implications,” he says. “But they are also, fundamentally, an act of civilisation.”

New panel is to find “fair and just solutions” for disputed works in museums

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

The 1:1 instant transfer from Chase Ultimate Rewards makes the Chase ecosystem your most efficient pipeline into World of Hyatt. The Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve both transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. Pair either with the Chase Freedom Unlimited or Chase Freedom Flex to funnel everyday spending into the UR ecosystem before converting to Hyatt points when you have a target booking.

Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. A room at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme during Paris Fashion Week might run $2,000/night while your award costs the same 25,000 points as a Tuesday in November. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#9169. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

So you just got a tattoo — congrats! Time to focus on aftercare. If you want your tattoo to age gracefully, the next few weeks are extra important to…

There are a number of reasons a new or old tattoo can itch. Infections, allergic reactions, and preexisting skin conditions are just a few possible…

#9167. 10 Art Books to Curl Up With This November

Celia Paul’s latest essay collection from Venice, Salman Toor’s painted worlds, the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg, a new Roy Lichtenstein catalog for old fans, and more.

The publishing industry is already preparing for spring, but we're still stuck on all the delights and challenges of this fall's slate of art books. Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara recommends an exploration of Marxist revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg's secret garden of pressed plants, an art form in its own right; critic Natalie Weis sinks into painter Celia Paul's kinetic prose. Catalogs on Salman Toor, Roy Lichtenstein, and more to discover below. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, edited by Alex Da Corte and Meg Onli | Whitney Museum of American Art, November 3

In this publication, the Whitney frames its Roy Lichtenstein show as a “radical” picture as “never before,” made up of a “novel” selection that is “genuinely new” to an audience “newer than ever” (emphasis the museum’s). But the catalog, inspired by the composition notebooks the artist kept to gather inspirational clippings, doesn’t feel academic or overstuffed, and includes beautiful plates — in other words, it’s easy, clean, and classic, all the reasons we’ve always loved Lichtenstein. —Lisa Yin Zhang

Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice by Celia Paul | New York Review Books, November 17

Celia Paul writes much like she paints, excavating shimmering insights from familiar subjects, in prose that is as haunting and luminous as her portraits. In this memoir, she uses a Venetian residency to examine her relationship with her deceased husband, mother, and first lover (the unnamed Lucian Freud). Grief, guilt, death, and desire stalk the artist through the city’s narrow corridors; once more, Paul seeks self-knowledge through art, literature, and the act of painting. —Natalie Weis

Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond by Arlene Dávila | Duke University Press, October 13

Arlene Dávila begins where most mainstream criticism of Latinx art ends: by challenging the term itself. The professor and curator’s ninth book continues her decades-long critiques of perfunctory “Latinx representation” through shrewd essays on indie filmmakers, fashion designers, and artists — such as Edra Soto and Ela Troyano — who refuse the tropes imposed on their work and often operate outside of the Los Angeles and New York bubbles. Her insights are a reminder to question the narratives that “make Latinx culture palatable for mainstream culture,” to always dig deeper. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

#9166. A Midterm Election Guide for Artists and Arts Workers

Issues touching on arts funding, censorship, AI regulation, and more are at stake for the country’s cultural sectors across key Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races.

Midterms are tomorrow, marking the first nationwide election since President Donald Trump started his second term in the Oval Office. In the wake of Trump’s financial and ideological crackdowns on Smithsonian, unapproved pet projects around the US Capitol, devastation to cultural landscapes through border construction, and dozens of other policies targeting history and heritage, many will be lining up at the polls with arts and culture policies on their minds.

Because Congress ultimately decides appropriations for federal arts entities, such as the National Endowment for the Arts, control of the House and Senate is incredibly important for the cultural sector. (Republicans currently have narrow majorities in both chambers.) From artists running for Congress, like Claire Valdez in New York and musician Bobby Pulido in Texas, to longtime culture advocates like Angie Nixon in the Senate race, we zeroed in on some of the key campaigns to watch in the United States if you care about artistic freedom, affordability for artists, and cultural funding.

We've organized this guide into three sections: Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races. Click through each section below.

Rebecca Schiffman and Lisa Yin Zhang also contributed to this guide.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by an average of five points in one of this election cycle’s most-anticipated races. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and the former head of the Detroit and Wayne County health departments, has been subject to repeated racism and culture war tirades over his Muslim faith and criticism of Israel by Rogers and President Trump throughout his campaign. Rogers, a former FBI agent and United States Representative, was endorsed by Trump in July 2025 and has received major funding from pro-Israel lobbying groups during this election cycle.

#9163. An expert’s guide to Pierre-Auguste Renoir: five must-read books on the French Impressionist

Pierre-Auguste Renoir's Self-Portrait (around 1875) © Clark Art Institute

• Click here for more reading lists on the world's greatest artists

The French Impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir is a surprisingly divisive artist, from some of his peers denigrating him to the so-called Renoir Sucks at Painting movement a decade ago and a critic recently labelling him “the chocolate boxiest” of the Impressionists. But the recently opened exhibition Renoir and Love at the National Gallery in London (which debuted at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris earlier this year and will travel to Boston in 2027) has had—for the most part—rave reviews and robust ticket sales. Its co-curator Christopher Riopelle, who is also the author of Renoir: The Great Bathers (1990), has selected five key books for anyone wanting to go beyond first impressions.

Renoir’s painting Madame Monet and Her Son (1874) depicts the artist’s wife and his son Jean, who would go on to write a book about his father as well as becoming a successful film-maker National Gallery of Art (Washington DC)

“Father and son, both artistic geniuses—a rare combination. That the great cineaste Jean Renoir should have penned an idiosyncratic, anecdote-filled life of the father is more than we deserve. Moreover, it is a film-maker’s biography, countless scenes set up visually, in flowing time. No surprise to learn that the loving son wrote it in far-off Hollywood!”

“Colin B. Bailey is our leading Renoir scholar. It is invidious to choose which of his several publications to include; I settle on this study of 69 portraits. Bulging with new information, it is every bit as indispensable to social historians as to art historians. As Renoir studies resurge, let us hope it returns to print.”

“Late Renoir: Marmite. But the period includes among its admirers Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso and the collector Albert C. Barnes. Sylvie Patry guides us through the final two decades with concision, deep respect and an unfailing eye for bravura painting. More than that, she demonstrates why the allusive Classicism of the late works played a key role in Modernism.”

“The Renoir scholar John House wrote this assessment of the largest and greatest of all Renoir collections with a passionate and utterly engaged eye. Martha Lucy was with him all the way; it’s as if we eavesdrop on a wickedly clever conversation between receptive student and brilliant, probing master.”

“At last, a meticulous scholarly edition of 314 key Renoir letters tracing his career from 1865 to 1919. Helped in shaping by the consummate Renoir scholar Anne Distel, finally we can ‘hear’ the master’s voice. The wit is clear but so, too, the anxiety. Let us have a translation soon, to stand beside the newly translated Claude Monet letters.”

• Renoir and Love, National Gallery, London, until 31 January 2027; Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 28 February 2027-13 June 2027

#9162. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#9158. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

#9156. Hard Truths: Should a Jilted Artist Keep Applying for Grants?

With a world in crisis and an art market spinning out of control, ace art-world consultants Chen & Lampert deliver hard truths in response to questions sent by Art in America readers from far and wide.

Last year you answered a reader’s question about grants, and it really got me thinking. I’m a mid-career artist with 25 years of exhibitions in respected galleries and art spaces. I never pursued grants or residencies earlier in my career, and as a result my credentials might appear thin. Your response prompted me to apply for a number of different grants, but so far nothing has worked out. Doing all this paperwork is actually pretty depressing. I feel like I gave it a go and should move on, but there’s a part of me that wants to keep at it despite my low chances. Is it worth it to keep trying? Related Articles Hard Choices: Is Our Advice Helpful? Hard Truths: Can Senior Citizens Be Sage Social-Media Ambassadors?

Once you’ve double-checked the project budget and resized JPEGs to the required DPI, your anxiety and acid reflux start acting up as you wonder: What if my application is declined? How will I make my work without a grant? At this point you’ve held steady for a quarter-century and managed to survive without hard-earned handouts. It appears that what you really desire is support, by which we mean acknowledgement from peers, panelists, and the extended Guggenheim family. But also, of course, a comically oversized check that can actually be deposited in a real FDIC-insured bank.

There is no shake-and-bake recipe for getting a grant, aside from the not-so-secret herbs and spices that are nepotism and cronyism. Lacking these ingredients, you still need to fry up a concise application that thoughtfully demonstrates the timeliness and urgency of your proposed project. Make sure to emphasize your decades of experience and demonstrate how grant-givers’ support will substantially bolster your vision at this crucial juncture. Don’t focus on dates, names, or details listed on the attached CV; instead, gush to them about compelling new ideas and your enthusiasm for building on previous accomplishments. They’d have to be cretinous schmucks not to want to help you grow.

You may opt to give up … or you could keep sending in the same, lightly touched-up application every grant season. Chances are they’ll eventually be forced to acknowledge you. This probably sounds outlandish, but we know rejectees who’ve doggedly hounded the same foundations for years and years until finally nabbing their award. If you think this is obnoxious and demeaning, remember that many of our most visible and rewarded artists are also our most tenacious naggers. Major funding organizations essentially recognize that you won’t stop applying, and whether they truly believe in your mission, they may ultimately greenlight a grant to make you go far, far away.

I work in the storage area at a gallery and while reshelving things I dropped a painting. No one saw it happen. The piece was wrapped with foam, but a corner got dinged. The art is just going back on the rack for the time being, so do I have to tell my boss? They’ll discover it eventually, but by then I won’t be working here anymore.

Here’s how we suspect this will go: It may be weeks, months or even years, but the discoverer of the damaged painting won’t care enough to investigate what happened. Sure, the gallerist will be miffed, but what’s new about that? An art handler (who, like you, won’t last long) will deliver the canvas to a framer for repair or replacement. They’ll charge a small fortune, but that’s par for the course because the bill—along with charges for the opening dinner, the e-flux ad, bubble wrap, and all other operational costs the gallery can tack on—will all be deducted from the artist’s cut of the sale. Or, just as likely, the piece will continue collecting dust until doomsday. By that point you’ll have far more pressing things to attend to, like finding potable water and not getting mowed down by bloodthirsty Waymo cabs. The karmic butterfly effect of one busted frame is nothing to fret about considering what’s coming.

#9155. Six concept vehicles from Stellantis exploring the future of car design

A Fiat that converts from a family car into a pickup and a Peugeot with a glass-bubble roof were among six concept cars unveiled by Stellantis at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, as captured in this video carousel by Dezeen.

Automotive corporation Stellantis unveiled the six concepts at a preview event in Meudon, outside Paris, on the eve of the motor show, offering an early look at the designs before the exhibition opened to the public.

The concepts explored different approaches to future car design – from reworking historic models to experimenting with colour-changing paint and illuminated bodywork.

Among the cars presented was Fiat’s Multiplay, which combines the proportions of a family vehicle with the functionality of a pickup.

Measuring 4.45 metres long, the concept has a sliding rear section that converts its six-seat-plus-one configuration into a four-seat vehicle with an open cargo bed.

Inside, a front passenger seat called the Sunseat folds into a lounge-style position beneath the panoramic roof, while a modular Petsenger seat can accommodate a pet, a child seat or storage.

The concept was finished in bright green, with a pink floor and red and pink upholstery inspired by the colours of a watermelon.

Citroën revisited its 1948 2CV with a compact electric concept featuring an orange-red body, grey steel wheels and yellow accents.

Inside, yellow tartan upholstery echoes details of the original model, while a fabric sunroof and removable storage basket replaced some of the conventional fittings found in modern cars.

The concept also features a detachable radio called Radioën, which doubles as a portable speaker, as well as door compartments designed to hold eggs, echoing the practical requirements of the original car.

Peugeot presented its RCZ Vision concept, a low-slung coupe with a sculpted body and a glass roof with a distinctive double-bubble profile that extends from the bonnet towards the rear.

Slim horizontal headlights reinterpret the brand’s three-claw motif, while a rear spoiler deploys only when the car is moving, keeping the bodywork smooth when parked.

Inside, a square steering control called Hypersquare replaces a conventional steering wheel and transparent micro-LED displays provide driving information while reducing the visual prominence of screens.

DS Automobiles’ F3VER concept features a compact body finished in Cosmic Blue paint that changes from vivid blue to violet depending on the light.

Its two-tone finish wraps around the rear of the car, while vertical Y-shaped headlights frame the front emblem.

At the rear, 16 LED panels sit within a sculptural light assembly informed by the vaulted roof of Paris’s Grand Palais.

Opel’s STX Concept is an electric estate car with a low roofline, sharply creased bonnet and sloping rear. Its front grille, known as the Vizor, incorporates vertical animated lights around an illuminated Opel emblem.

The rear bumper features extendable aerodynamic elements, while glass light strips run from the rear side windows into the roof.

Cameras replace conventional wing mirrors and three-section alloy wheels are designed to improve aerodynamic efficiency.

Alfa Romeo’s Cuorerosso concept car explores the brand’s future sports-car design through a streamlined body, active air intakes and slim aerodynamic mirrors.

Its rear window echoes the shape of the brand’s triangular front grille, while the interior is organised around the driver, with controls concealed in the central console until needed.

Stellantis was formed in 2021 through the merger of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles and France’s PSA Group.

Its portfolio includes Alfa Romeo, Citroën, DS Automobiles, Fiat, Opel and Peugeot, among other automotive brands.

#9154. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#9153. In Fiery Court Filing, Democratic Lawmaker Says Kennedy Center’s Closure Is Meant to Hide Its Failure Under Trump

The much-debated potential two-year closure of the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts is being proposed to cover up the institution’s failings since US president Donald Trump installed loyalists to the board and became its chair, says Ohio Democrat Joyce Beatty in a fiery 51-page Friday filing in US District Court for Washington, D.C. Beatty is an ex-officio member of the board of trustees. Trump has insisted the closure is necessary and dictated a date for it, the filing points out, without any proper board oversight.

The strongly worded filing says the administration has responded “grudgingly—to put it generously” to requests for information; criticizes a defense by Trump as being based on “a fake one-year review that never happened”; cites a “sham process to lend a false patina of legitimacy”; and, in a piquant choice of words given Trump’s admiration of the Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, calls Trump’s decision to close the center a “ukase,” a term referring to a proclamation by a tsar. All that is on page one. Related Articles Former Presidents Obama, Clinton Mock Trump's White House Interiors With Comparisons to 'Saddam Hussein' and 'Liberace's Bathroom' Donors Are Secretly Trying to Save the Kennedy Center's Artworks from 'Destruction' or Disposal Amid Trump Takeover

The Kennedy Center referred ARTnews’s request for comment on the filing to the Department of Justice, which did not immediately respond.

Charles Matthew Floca, facilities manager, was charged with finding a consultant “to bless Trump’s closure decision,” says the filing. Only the Delta Consulting Group applied, and the group was required to provide a recommendation within just days. The board approved Trump’s decision to close the center on August 13, 2025, and, says the filing, only received Delta’s written report on August 31, two weeks later. “The bizarre timeline says it all,” says the filing.

The board then held another vote on September 15, seemingly indicating the insufficiency of the first one, and, says the filing, preparatory materials were provided to participants just three days before. It contained serious inaccuracies, says the filing, including that congressionally appropriated funds for the center’s renovation must be spent by September 2029, which Beatty says is false, pointing out that the funds can be spent through September 2034.

The “kicker,” says the filing, is that Floca and others told trustees that construction costs would double, increasing by more than $300 million, if a phased approach to repairs were implemented. Meanwhile, letters from real estate services company Jones Lang LaSalle, called upon to outline the schedule for renovations, make clear that “Delta’s estimates were exaggerated,” but those letters were not shared with the trustees.

The two-year closure plan, says the filing, “was designed, not in good faith for the best interests of the Center, but to cover up Defendants’ own mismanagement and to please Trump.”

The filing says that the organization’s chief financial officer texted Floca on September 10, saying, “We need to get shut” because “we are burning money,” memorializing statements by the board’s vice chair, Jennifer Fischer, in a conversation with US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick. She also said that “opponents [will] say [prior Kennedy Center president Richard] Grenell raised a ton of money and then we burned it to the ground.”

The timeline, says the filing, is transparently motivated by Trump’s desire to preside over the reopening. As Lutnick himself said outside the courthouse ahead of a hearing, “why would the President agree to work on the restoration where he’s going to be the President for the next… two-and-a-half years, and then he’s leaving?”

Trump fired the longtime board chair in February 2025 and stocked the board with supporters, and was swiftly elected chair by the new board members; Floca was appointed in March 2026 though he “lacks arts management expertise.”

Attendance and donations then dropped significantly. In December 2025, the board announced it would add Trump’s name to the center, a move Beatty sued to stop. Artists canceled scheduled performances and ticket sales dropped by as much as 70 percent, notes the filing. Trump announced on February 1, 2026 that “I have determined” that the center would close on July 4 and cease operations to allow for a two-year renovation, citing a “one year review” with experts. “No such review ever happened,” says Beatty’s filing.

Congress had appropriated $257 million for upkeep of the building in 2025, with construction phased out over time and the center remaining open. Floca initially said he recommended the two-year closure in January 2026, and has testified that the duration was set by Trump in a message on his social media platform, Truth Social. Beatty amended her suit to stop the closure and requested information to evaluate the validity of the decision. Defendants failed to provide information just days before a scheduled March 16 vote, she says, resulting in the court issuing an order requiring defendants to hand over materials. But no such materials had even been prepared, says the filing.

By the time the meeting came, Trump said it was “too late for the board” to object “because we’ve already announced the closure.” Trustee input was, he said, a “minor detail.”

Despite a court ruling prohibiting the closure, management wound down programming, says the filing. Foca claims he took no efforts to develop the 2026–27 season and even encouraged the National Symphony Orchestra to leave the campus, depriving the center of thousands of ticket sales. Staff layoffs continued.

Changing input from JLL, meantime, first indicated that total closure was necessary, but later revised its advice, saying phased renovations were feasible but also noting that the Kennedy Center’s “true needs approach $400–450 million.” Keeping the center open during the work would incur additional costs of $60 million–$80 million. The latter message was withheld from the trustees, says the filing.

The board then looked for a consultant to support the necessity of Trump’s proposed two-year closure. Only Delta Consulting Group applied, though, according to Beatty, it “lacked any expertise in performing arts management.” It was told to assume a two-year closure beginning with Trump’s decreed date of July 6. JLL’s revised assessment, saying the center could remain open during work, was not provided to Delta.

What’s more, documents included in the filing indicate that Lutnick “shaped the content of Delta’s presentation,” which stated that phased renovations would cost some $560 million, more than twice what Congress had appropriated. “Management knew that was not accurate,” says the filing, noting that JLL’s updated plan calculated only an additional cost of $41 million for a phased renovation.

Furthermore, the defendants produced JLL’s second, revised report only after the completion of depositions in the case, despite its relevance, says the filing, adding that Floca denied under questioning that any updated plan existed.

Heavy rains on September 4 caused the collapse of a small section of ceiling plaster in the foyer, which the center informed staff would result in closure for the rest of the day. Three days before the September 15 meeting, the board received new information, containing two draft resolutions. One again proposed adding Trump’s name to the building, saying that “certain fiscal collapse” would result if Trump were not recognized on the building’s facade as he could not be expected to provide oversight without receiving that distinction. “This was the first and only time that the full Board has been informed of the institution’s ‘certain fiscal collapse,’” says the filing. It also proposed once again that the board approve Trump’s plan to close for two years. It revealed for the first time that Delta and Floca considered the main building “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

Beatty appealed to the court and the renaming proposal was taken off the agenda.

Floca then told the trustees that phased work would double the cost, and the board voted for closure. Trump said that day on social media that the center would close immediately but that renovation couldn’t continue until the court ruled on the name change and that if it did not go through, the work would not take place.

Floca then announced on September 16 that the main building would need to close immediately for safety reasons. The same day, Trump told reporters that unless his name went on the facade, “it’s going to close, it will end up being ripped down.” The same night, a photographer captured an image of him on Air Force One, reading a placard that appeared to read “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

#9152. US and China share a love of "new things and innovation" says Ma Yansong

Chinese architect Ma Yansong has completed one of the highest-profile US buildings of 2026 – the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, in California. In this interview, he explains his architecture’s international appeal as a “bridge between imagination and reality”.

Speaking over video call on the occasion of the Lucas Museum’s opening, Ma told Dezeen that the building has acted as a stable point in a rapidly changing world, with trade wars, AI races and a US federal government that has enshrined classical architecture as a national norm.

“This project took 12 years, across two countries, and the world changed around it. The building didn’t,” he said.

The long-anticipated project, funded by Star Wars creator George Lucas, was first planned for San Francisco, then Chicago, before landing in Los Angeles.

“What made it possible is that George and I come from different roots, but both love the same kind of thing – stories that belong to ordinary people, not to high culture,” said Ma.

Ma believes this shared tendency toward exploration between himself and the American filmmaker applies more widely, and the 51-year-old architect spoke positively about the potential for architecture to illuminate the similarities between China and the United States.

“I see a lot in common between the two countries,” he said. “They both like innovation and new things, and they focus on young people, on education.”

“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality”

His own life mirrors this outlook. Attracted by innovation as a youth in Beijing, he travelled to Yale, where he graduated with a master’s degree in 2002.

At Yale, Ma became interested in Zaha Hadid’s parametric architecture and eventually worked at her firm in London.

Despite teaching and working mostly in the United States and Europe, Hadid cultivated her signature parametric style working in China’s early 2000s building boom.

The completion of the Lucas Museum represents a Chinese architect taking these principles abroad, a full-circle moment as Ma moved from the US to the UK, back to China, where he has completed dozens of projects, bringing his honed sensibility to California.

Buildings created in the parametric style, or design based on the specific geometries allowed by computer calculations, have been criticised for their lack of relation to sites, and for being self-referential.

The museum’s curved exterior is covered in thousands of white polymer panels, giving it a futuristic look.

Nevertheless, Ma pushes back on Dezeen’s description of the building as “spaceship-like”. Instead, he compares it to a cloud, as an enduring symbol for the imagination – an aspect of consciousness that the architect hopes is provoked by his buildings.

He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.

The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.

“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.

The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.

Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.

“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.

“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”

Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.

“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”

“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”

For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.

“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”

“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”

At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.

The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.

“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”

“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”

“I like the future, but not the cold future”

The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.

Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.

And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.

“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”

Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.

“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.

#9151. Czech Archaeologists Re-Excavate Long-Lost Tombs of Ancient Egyptian High Officials

Czech archaeologists working at Saqqara have re-excavated a group of tombs belonging to high priests and senior officials of Egypt’s Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BCE). The news was first reported by Ahram Online following an announcement by the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

Located 20 miles south of Cairo, the Saqqara archaeological site was the main necropolis for the ancient Egyptian city of Memphis, which was founded around 3100 BCE and abandoned in the 7th century CE. The excavations were made as part of a project by the Czech Institute of Egyptology to locate, excavate, and document tombs partially explored in the 19th century and buried again over time. Related Articles Monumental Statues of Ramses II Discovered in Egypt Ancient Fayum Mummy Portrait Gets Fresh Restoration, With Rare Plans to Leave Egypt for Italy

These tombs were first discovered by the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette, founder of the Egyptian Antiquities Service, between 1858 and 1860. During those years, Mariette identified approximately 160 tombs in the area dating to the Old Kingdom. However, his excavations focused largely on major artifacts while leaving other parts of the tombs unexplored and inadequately documented.

Among the chief monuments investigated by the Czech mission are the tombs of a man called Sabu and his son Ptahshepses, both of whom were high-ranking officials associated with the cult of Ptah at Memphis. The team also excavated and documented previously unknown parts of the tombs, including an offering chapel belonging to Sabu’s wife, Ikhetnefert, which was never found by Mariette.

Located north of the tomb of his son, Sabu’s tomb has exterior walls mimicking the facades of royal palaces, reflecting his high standing. Inside, researchers found well-preserved reliefs depicting Sabu and Ptahshepses overseeing processions of offering bearers.

Ikhetnefert’s chapel contains a false door decorated with scenes of Ikhetnefert with her husband and their two sons, Peahshepses and Raneferef. According to Miroslav Bárta, head of the Czech team, it is one of team’s most important discoveries, providing new insight into the family and its relationships.

The mission also succeeded in locating the tomb of Ptahshepses through a combination of satellite imagery and field surveys. Here, the archaeologists found the untouched remains of his mummy inside a limestone sarcophagus. Their subsequent analysis indicated that he was over 60 when he died, making him exceptionally long-lived for his time.

According to surviving written sources, Ptahshepses held senior positions under four Fifth Dynasty kings: Sahure, Neferirkare, Raneferef, and Nyuserre. He was the first non-royal to marry an Egyptian princess, Khamaat, daughter of King Userkaf, the founder of the Fifth Dynasty.

In a statement, Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that the significance of the Czech mission’s renewed investigation lies in its study and documentation of these monuments using modern scientific methods, which are revealing new information about the religious beliefs and social lives of Old Kingdom officials.
