#9150. Luminous viewpoint by Ryue Nishizawa rises within Japanese landfill site

Photography by Setouchi Art and Industry

A giant orange cone designed by Japanese architect Ryue Nishizawa acts as an observation platform at this large recycling complex on Shikoku island in Japan.

Nishizawa, co-founder of Japanese studio SANAA, positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin at Oono Associates, a recycling complex in the city of Toon, and open up this closed-off industrial space to the public.

Named Observatory, it was created for the inaugural edition of Setouchi Art and Industry 2026, an art and architecture festival held across industrial sites in Japan.

Specifically, it is part of the Landscapes of Waste – A landscape shaped by nature, industry, and people exhibition, curated by architect Kazuyo Sejima, who co-founded SANAA with Nishizawa in 1995.

Nishizawa positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin within the vast recycling complex in Toon, Ehime, revealing the closed-off industrial setting to the public.

The bright orange cone measures 33 metres in diameter and four metres in height. Its size was intended to emulate an artificial hill.

Its luminous orange finish was chosen to deliberately contrast the blue-green hues of the surrounding landfill lining and landscape beyond it.

The platform encourages visitors to observe how the landscape is shaped by nature and human activity, and experience the processes of material circulation at the recycling plant.

Alongside Nishizawa’s observation platform, the Landscapes of Waste exhibition includes bus stops by architectural studio Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa Otsubo, as well as a bus and visitor wear by architect Suzuko Yamada.

Visitors are required to take this bus to the site and put on the clothing, as seen in the photos. The festival team said this brings “visitors themselves into the composition of the landscape”.

“Together, these interventions invite a closer encounter with the relationship between nature, industrial infrastructure and human activity,” it added.

Setouchi Art and Industry 2026 was organised by the Japan Industrial Art Foundation. Artists and architects were invited to work with industrial sites across Okayama and the Ehime prefecture on Shikoku to create a “decentralised museum” that opens these settings to the public.

Its inaugural edition runs until 31 October across seven venues, which also include a salt production site, a textile factory, a shipbuilder and a battery manufacturer.

“Developed through collaboration between artists and participating companies, the exhibitions offer access to industrial spaces usually closed to the public, revealing the technologies, materials and people behind everyday life,” said Setouchi Art and Industry.

“We hope that many people, including the younger generation, will re-examine Japan’s industries from a fresh perspective and discover the charm and potential hidden within them,” added Japan Industrial Art Foundation director Masahiro Ito.

Other recent projects by SANAA include the Taichung Green Museumbrary in Taiwan and a proposal for the National Museum of Ecuador.

Observatory: Ryue NishizawaPlaza (roundabout, forest path, elevated path, rest area) and bus stop: Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa OtsuboBus and visitor wear: Suzuko Yamada (in collaboration with Kazuya Suzuki, Posa)Supervision: Kazuyo SejimaAdvisors: Yuko Hasegawa, Yusuke Okura, Atsuhiro MiyakeBus video cinematographer: Kenji AgataBus video music and sound engineering: Takayuki Noami (Non-REM Studio)

#9149. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

#9148. Tattoo Enthusiasts Have One More Week to Get a Rembrandt Inked for $400 or Less

Fans of both body art and the Dutch Golden Age have one more week to book an appointment for a Rembrandt-themed tattoo at the Rembrandt House Museum.

The museum—located in the artist’s former canal-side home in central Amsterdam—is halfway through a two-week public event called “The Poor Man’s Rembrandt Project,” organized with the renowned 74-year-old Dutch tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher and his studio. (The Rembrandt House Museum held a similar event with Schiffmacher in 2023.) Related Articles London's National Gallery to Exhibit 40 Works, From Rembrandt to René Magritte Van Gogh Museum Reaches Agreement with Dutch Government on Contentious Renovation Budget

This fall’s event wraps up on November 7, and at press time, slots are still available with Schiffmacher or one of the six other tattoo artists who have opened up a temporary studio in the museum. Clients can book sessions ranging from 100 to 350 euros, or about $110 to $390, and choose from any number of designs culled from Rembrandt’s drawings and etchings.

Options include one of the artist’s recognizable self-portraits; a palette adorned with Amsterdam’s triple-X coat of arms; Hansken, the famous elephant that Rembrandt drew when she toured Amsterdam; and a number of other figure groupings and scenes.

As part of the project, Schiffmacher put out a call for someone willing to have Rembrandt’s The Descent from the Cross tattooed onto his back. About 50 people expressed interest, Schiffmacher told the New York Times, but many had scars or birthmarks that would interfere with the design. Enter production designer Bo Kwakernaak, a “completely clean, young man with a beautiful back,” according to Schiffmacher. He and his colleagues have been collaborating on the post-Crucifixion scene over several sessions.

The museum doesn’t see this public tattooing event as a gimmick. Epco Runia, the Rembrandt House’s head of collections and research, thinks there is a real connection between the prints Rembrandt made (which make up most of the museum’s permanent collection) and the art of tattooing, in that both are effective tools of image dissemination. “I think [Rembrandt] would have some kind of click with Henk Schiffmacher,” Runia told the Times. “They have a little bit the same kind of character.”

A burger chain's pixel-art RPG has gamers excited, and there are good reasons for that.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’d told me a decade ago that Wendy's would release one of the most talked-about indie RPGs of 2026, I’d have assumed your burger had some dodgy mushrooms. Yet here we are: it's actually happening.

The world's third-largest hamburger fast-food chain has unveiled a turn-based, pixel-art adventure in which its red-haired mascot leads a party of fast-food heroes to save a kingdom in peril. It's called WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones. No, this is not a South Park parody. This is a real, playable game.

The branded element isn't just about bigging up Wendy's either: it also takes potshots at rivals. In the game, for example, your enemies include Frydusa, a carton of snake-like French fries, and a gang called the Golden Archers. As a dig at McDonald’s, it's not subtle.

81monkeys, an indie studio in Port Moody, British Columbia, is making the game, and it’s heading to Steam. You might expect something so obviously corporate to either get trounced on social media or get ignored and sink without a trace. At the time of writing, though, gamers mostly seem to be asking… why it looks so good.

There's more. Last summer, Pepsi asked on social media whether it should make a video game. It was buried in replies pointing out that it already had. One came from Kotaro Uchikoshi, now a celebrated visual-novel director (yes, that's a thing now), who'd worked on 1999’s Pepsiman and was offering to reconnect the company with the original team.

Branded games are clearly back on the menu. The question is… why? Well, first it's worth noting that we've been here before.

Domino’s Avoid the Noid in 1989 is widely cited as the first fast-food tie-in game. McDonald’s followed with Global Gladiators, which is considered one of the best platformers of its era. Then there was Cool Spot, starring the red dot from 7 Up’s American logo, which you could play on the SNES and Mega Drive in 1993 and, branding tie-in aside, is a genuinely brilliant 2D platform game.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The original Pepsiman, though, remains the king of the branded games. Released only in Japan (which always helps cult status), it showed a superhero sprinting through cities to deliver Pepsi cans. And it remains much-loved: these days, copies go for hundreds of dollars on sites like eBay.

Then came Burger King's 2006 experiment. The chain sold three branded Xbox games for $3.99, including the infamous stealth title Sneak King, as long as you bought a value meal (sold separately). BK ended up shifting more than 3.2 million copies in total.

KFC was late to the party, only joining the fun in 2019 with I Love You, Colonel Sanders! A Finger Lickin’ Good Dating Simulator. The parody dating sim got flayed by critics, but players loved it, giving it a 91% positive rating on Steam.

From a branding perspective, what's interesting is that these weren’t just adverts with gameplay bolted on. They were proper games that people actually liked, even if reviewers were somewhat sniffy. So why are they coming back now? It's difficult to say, but I think a few factors are in play.

First, the original branded games' child audience is now an adult audience with money, and nostalgia is a powerful force. Second, it’s far easier to distribute games today. While Burger King once had to manufacture physical copies and distribute them to restaurants, now Wendy’s just needs a Steam page.

Thirdly, traditional advertising is struggling to break through ad blockers, ad-free subscriptions and a general lack of interest. In contrast, people actually like a branded game. They might even actively seek it out.

Finally, there's the backlash against AI. Wendy's Steam page proudly declares its game “100% fresh and 100% human-made” for a reason. As we all drown in AI slop, handcrafted, indie-style pixel art becomes a visual statement of brand values.

None of this, of course, guarantees that these games will succeed. For every Global Gladiators there’s a Sneak King, a game remembered more as a curio than for its gameplay. The brands that get this right treat players as players, not targets for ads.

So will WendyQuest join Pepsiman in the hall of fame, or end up in the bargain bin of history? I have no clue. But if a burger chain can get me excited about a turn-based RPG, its marketing team must be doing something right. And Pepsi, if you’re reading: Uchikoshi’s offer is still on the table.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9146. Remembering Dolores Huerta: Artists Barbara Carrasco, Judith F. Baca, Yreina D. Cervántez, and Vincent Valdez Reflect on the Iconic Activist’s Legacy

“It’s hard to believe this amazing icon is gone from our world,” artist Judith F. Baca said of Dolores Huerta, the labor activist who died last week at 96.

A cofounder of the United Farm Workers of America, Huerta is best-known for her decades-long dedication to fighting for the labor rights of farmworkers in the fields of California and more broadly for helping to galvanize the Chicano civil rights movement. She recruited members to the union’s cause, led strikes and ensured that companies felt the impact of the absence of the farmworkers whom they exploited, and negotiated the contracts that provided material change to the lives and working conditions for campesinos and campesinas. “She turned the phrase ‘Sí, se puede!’ into a chant that animated rallies and marches well into a new century,” as the Los Angeles Times put it.

“She was always conscious of having women be at the table,” artist Barbara Carrasco told ARTnews, noting that as a UFW negotiator Huerta, one of the few women in a leadership position, was labeled “the dragon lady” for her fierceness. Carrasco said she will always remember Huerta as a nurturing figure who mentored countless women over the decades.

After leaving UFW in the 1980s, she would continue to advocate for labor rights and women rights. In 2002, Huerta received the Puffin Prize for Creative Citizenship, which came with a $100,000 grant. She decided to use the funds start her an eponymous foundation, which aims to “cultivate empowered volunteer organizations actively pursuing social justice,” according to its website.

Huerta’s status as an icon has also translated into the art world, with numerous artists depicting her image over the years, including Baca, Carrasco, Yreina D. Cervántez, and Vincent Valdez, all of whom share their memories of Huerta below.

b. 1955, El Paso, Texas; lives and works in Los Angeles

I first met Dolores when I was around 19. My boyfriend at the time was UCLA student, and I heard Cesar Chavez speak on campus, and I was really impressed. I met Dolores right after, and never in my life, I have met a more charismatic lady. She was just so down to earth. That’s what always struck me about her: Here is this woman with all these accolades are given to her, but she still is such a great human being. She’d meet people—it didn’t matter if they were rich or poor—and she’d treat them all the same. I think that’s what struck a lot of us; we would just say, “Oh, this lady’s amazing.” I went to an UFW convention once, and so many farmworkers came up to her, and they just loved her. That doesn’t happen overnight. That takes years and years of dedication and of being out there and representing them. There’s a quote by her: “Every moment is an organizing opportunity, every person a potential activist, every minute a chance to change the world.” I think she really did take advantage of her time here on Earth.

I’m one of many, many women whom she nurtured and helped. There are so many women, from women in public office to women working in the fields. She always had such pride in the women she mentored. She was also very supportive of visual artists. I remember the night before an event for the Department of Labor, when Hilda Solis was secretary, Dolores asked me to write a list of all the artists who had contributed to the UFW over the years. During the event, she mentioned everybody. I thought, Who does that? Not too many people will pay tribute to the artists. The artist are often the last individuals to be thanked [in a political movement].

In the ’90s, Self-Help Graphics did a women’s atelier [series of prints]. I invited 10 women to join, and I remember saying we should do a print showing women as nurturers. I wanted to pay tribute to Dolores—that was who came to mind immediately. When you do something and you really truly believe in it, it shows. I truly loved her, and I wanted to show that. The colors were specifically chosen: the yellow ocher reflects the good energy coming from her, the blue-green background represents the fields and the farmworkers she was defending in those fields, the rose represents her strength and beauty, both inward and outward. I always thought she was so beautiful and a beautiful soul, too. It was a work I didn’t rush. I was so happy when the Girl Scouts of America selected that portrait to be on a merit patch.

Dolores had a good sense of humor. That was one of our big connections. She and I used to laugh about really silly stuff—if I told you, you wouldn’t believe what we were laughing about it. She always said to keep your inner child alive and not to ignore it. I think that’s why she was able to laugh with so many people and get along with everybody. Her energy was always high, even until the end. We partied together like crazy. At my 70th birthday last year, Dolores was dancing—she loved to dance. She said if she didn’t do what she did, she would have been a dancer.

The last time I talked to her on the phone was about two weeks ago. I got a chance to tell her that I loved her. A lot of us who have been friends with her were lucky enough to see her right before she started treatment. It took her faster than everybody thought. I know firsthand what that kind of treatment is like; I’ve been cancer-free now for some 30 years, and I remember how brutal that kind of treatment is, and I was young, and she was 96. It’s got to be really difficult. She told me she was in a lot of pain. Even though we knew the day was coming soon, it was still a sad day for all of us. She was one of those people who was extremely energetic. When everybody would be tired, she would say, “Come on, let’s do this, and let’s do that.” It was inspiring to be around her.

b. 1946, Los Angeles; lives and works in Los Angeles

Early on in the movement, Dolores and I would have been present at similar things, marches and organizing events in support of the United Farm Workers. I was also at La Paz working at one point [around 1974] to produce a big mural that Carlos Almaraz had designed. I remember painting a section that said, “No More Sweetheart Contacts,” and that piece was used for a march to Sacramento. The making of that giant canvas was the first time I went to La Paz. I might have met her then, but I knew her from a distance for a while. I can’t quite remember when I started to have more personal contact with her.

At a certain point, I had a chance to speak with Dolores at length, and she told me that she was not given the credit that she was due as a cofounder of the United Farm Workers and for the work that she had done. Of course, I understood that because I had struggled myself with the dominance of men within the mural movement and the Chicano movement, and in the art world as well. So, when I started working on Arch of Dignity, Equality and Justice (2005–08), which is a 25-foot arch on the campus of San Jose State University, I decided when I was going to put Dolores in the front of the monument—that she would be the dominant figure, not Chavez. I depicted her in a thoughtful way: One of her hands is outstretched, saying, “Join me,” and is welcoming, and the other hand is a fist. In other words, she was both those things simultaneously. It is a depiction of her in leadership role, coming up out of the fields. From that point on, when I was making something historical, I looked to Dolores as a way to represent the power of a Chicana organizer and a model for us in social activism. In a sense, she was a hero for me over and over again.

She had the most amazing energy I ever experienced—never tiring. Not only that, but you could end up dancing all night with her. I remember staying up until three in the morning with her listening to music at Burning Man in the tent. I have a fabulous image of her in a dust storm there. I couldn’t even get out of the car; it was so horrible. I put my head out and I was choking, and there she was standing there laughing. I thought, How did she get that tenacity, that resilience? It must have been from being out in the Central Valley and having dealt with bad conditions like that in the field. So that to me was a real image of her resilience and her capacity to withstand any storm.

In Gente del Maíz (2012) for the Miguel Contreras Learning Center, you see Dolores in the fields [on the left] with a bullhorn. That comes from a story that Maria Elena Durazo [then executive vice president of the national AFL-CIO Executive Council] told me about how Dolores had called Miguel Contreras to join the United Farm Workers. Later, of course, he joined the United Farm Workers and led the Delano Grape Boycott in Canada. I wanted to indicate that here was this young man, Miguel, who didn’t have a plan to become an activist. It was through Dolores’s encouragement that he joined the movement, and he became a critical figure in it. The central image is an ear of corn with three figures: a young Miguel drops soil, another drops kernels in the soil, and the other is watering the soil. Out of these planted corn kernels come community organizers. I was talking about how there’s the planting of people, the nurturing of souls that become engaged in in a passionate commitment to social justice. I think that’s what Dolores models for us repeatedly: a lifelong commitment to social justice. That’s something important for young people to learn, because they often don’t have an understanding of what it takes to commit a life to creating change. I think more young people need to learn activism is something that you put your body on the line. Dolores was arrested around 25 times, and she was beaten almost to death in San Francisco by the police and they ruptured her spleen. Dolores put her body, her heart, and her spirit into the movement.

In Seeing Through Others’ Eyes (2010), she is there between Chavez and Robert F. Kennedy leading the crowd, while these two men break bread. It’s important to say that we can’t let the discussion of Dolores Huerta focus on her being victimized by Cesar Chavez. It cannot be about that because that’s a diminishment of her character. She was much larger and much more powerful than simply a rape victim.

Dolores was a model, not only training young people to become activists but also she’s a model for standing up against the most powerful forces. I don’t think I can think of a person who can replace her or that can equal her contributions. She’s the Chicana icon, and she will be sorely missed. She was one of the greatest leaders we’ve had.

b. 1952, Garden City, Kansas; lives and works in Los Angeles

It has been my honor and privilege to know Dolores Huerta, whose influence on me and so many others have been tremendous. Dolores has been a warrior in the best sense of the word: powerful, resilient, compassionate, harnessing her formidable intelligence to fight for the rights of those most vulnerable. Dolores was a feminista, a great humanitarian, resolute, and committed for the long term in the struggle for justice and a better world.

Dolores Huerta has had an impact on many generations of women and men, but she had a very special significance for young Chicanas and Latinas of my generation. Before now there were virtually no positive images of women like us in film or media. She was such an inspiration as one of the first prominent mujeres of our time that was a public figure and activista. Dolores showed us courage and dedication, and what it meant to fight for our dignity, equal rights, and how to show solidarity with diverse peoples and struggles.

I met Dolores in Santa Cruz in the early ’70s when I was student, but I did not get to know her until the ’80s. One of my first encounters with her was in East LA. I was asked to help out for a UFW function organized by Fred Ross Jr. and Dolores was there. We had an opportunity to talk at length. I am grateful for that experience and other times spent in her presence; she was very generous and approachable. I last spoke with Dolores at the birthday party for artist Barbara Carrasco, her dear friend. Dolores looked radiant, peaceful, as always composed. I cherish the memory of her dancing—joyful, celebrating, mighty.

Dolores was a strong advocate for the arts and artists. I am very grateful for the support she showed me and many other artists, especially the mujeres artistas. My heartfelt dedication to Dolores Huerta came in the form of the mural La Ofrenda. Located in the Echo Park community, it was created as part of my graduate thesis at UCLA (sponsored by SPARC and the City of Los Angeles Cultural Affairs Department). The mural was executed with the assistance of talented mural crew(s) with contributions from Salvadoran poet Rossana Perez, Chicana/o poets Gloria Enedina Alvarez, Victor Carrillo, and graffiti artist Eric “Duke” Montenegro. Originally painted in 1989, it is meant as an offering to my community, a prayer to the ancestors for courage, strength, and sustenance. It is about the value of labor, the farmworkers, immigration, political exile, and very importantly Chicanx solidarity with the people of Central and Latin America and their wars for liberation. La Ofrenda highlights the vital role of women in creating transformative change. I thought it most fitting to honor Dolores as the central figure in the mural, a unifying force across many cultures, struggles, and advocate for many just causes.

Unfortunately, many of the issues La Ofrenda depicted almost 40 years ago, including the victimization and persecution of immigrants in the US and worldwide persists with unimaginable cruelty. Let us follow the example of Dolores and make “good trouble” as she did in her lifetime and continue to fight for the rights of immigrants, farmworkers, women, and all people. It is my hope that La Ofrenda be a reminder and inspiration to those that knew Dolores Huerta and those that will learn of her enduring legacy, and immeasurable contributions to humanity. So much love and gratitude to you Dolores, beloved mujer and hermana. You are siempre presente.

b. 1977, San Antonio, Texas; lives and works in Houston and San Antonio

There was no better way to begin my ACLU project, The New Americans (2026), than with Dolores Huerta. Dolores’s legacy remains a powerful testament and reminder—our current struggles are nothing new. Generations before us have long endured and remained steadfast in their commitment to confront and challenge the distorted social realities within the United States. Although my portrait of Dolores intends to pay respect to the elders, it is strategic in its conceptual pose. Despite her age, Dolores’s resilient spirit still burns bright. Her head holds high. She is caught gazing optimistically toward the right side of the page. As the first image in a series of 25 drawings, she leads us forward, eager to hand off the torch to those willing to come next. Dolores Huerta will forever be that reminder to us all—be the stubborn pulse in a dying heart.

The first time Dolores and I met in 2015 was completely random and somewhat surreal. It was a very late night after party in Berlin, after the Berlin Film Festival. It was already 2 a.m. And I left before she did. We met up again in 2023 at the Rothko Chapel in Houston. We sat on a stage together with Cheech Marin and shared stories and ideas together about the intertwining of art and democracy. By the end of the discussion, Dolores had managed to convince the entire audience to stand on their feet. She had several hundred people and a mostly white audience, shouting in unison from the tops of their lungs, “SI SE PUEDE!!” Cheech and I stared and smirked at each other in complete awe.

I last saw Dolores in 2024. We met at LACMA to view my exhibition, “El Chavez Ravine.” We spent a memorable afternoon together. I snuck Dolores a razor blade out of my pocket and asked her to etch her name into the back of the lowrider ice cream truck that was the centerpiece of the exhibition. Her spirit of rebellion was always ready, it seemed. At the tail end of the day, I expressed my idea to create a portrait of her in hopes of using it as a catalyst one day, for a bigger idea. I photographed her hands and face before we parted ways.

And finally, just [last Tuesday], I mailed Dolores a personal letter and package containing her portrait along with the completed series of drawings, The New Americans. [On Wednesday] morning, I heard the news. There is something bittersweet about the thought of this envelope never being opened and read by her. Her spirit was a powerful, magnetic force in life and, now, in memory.

#9144. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

As they lift our gaze from our phones, we'll start looking up.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Did you ever see the 2021 Leonardo DiCaprio film Don't Look Up? I don't think it's a spoiler to say that its focus on people not looking up was partly a satire on climate change denial. But more broadly, it fed into the idea that nowadays, we're all looking down a lot; specifically at our phones.

I've honestly got no idea if smart glasses – some of which can now project information, images and videos straight at your eyeballs – will end up taking off in future, and replacing the smartphone. But if they do, then it occurs to me that this will be big news for billboards.

You might assume that if more digital tech catches on, physical advertising would be one of the casualties. After all, why look at a poster when your glasses can show you something tailored? But the more I think about it, the more convinced I am the opposite will happen.

Consider this: nobody is going to wear smart glasses to look at their feet. The whole attraction is that you get the benefits of a phone while keeping your eyes on the world around you. And in most towns and cities – even in this smartphone era – that world is already plastered with outdoor advertising.

And if smart glasses can truly take advantage of augmented reality – tech that overlays digital content onto real-world, physical things – then those billboards will suddenly be a lot more exciting to look at.

For over a century, billboards have been essentially a one-way medium. QR codes promised to fix that, but how many of us have actually stopped in the street, taken out our phones and waggled them at a pixelated square? Once or twice, maybe. But on a regular basis? Hardly.

In future, I reckon, you'll be able to point smart glasses at a billboard and get it to do all sorts of useful things, probably by talking to an AI bot embedded in your specs.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

With a movie billboard, for instance, you might want to play the trailer or find out which cinema it's playing at nearby, and when. You might even want turn-by-turn directions to the multiplex to appear in front of your very eyes.

This might sound like Black Mirror-style sci-fi, but it's worth remembering how many old Black Mirror episodes have essentially come true already. And it certainly seems to be the way the ad industry is thinking.

In fact, you can already see a version of this idea in east London. Electric Garden, on Shoreditch High Street, bills itself as “the billboard you can walk into”. It’s a 21,000 sq ft open-air site that sits behind a row of giant digital screens, so brands can run a campaign on the screens and then build a physical world behind them for people to explore.

Its launch campaign, for Activision’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, turned the site into a neon-lit, Seoul-inspired alleyway, complete with convenience stores, plastic stools and code-breaking missions. As co-founder Alex Ezen puts it: “A screen can capture attention, but a physical experience gives people a reason to stop, take part and share it.”

Smart glasses could deliver something similar without anyone needing to build an alleyway. That will make the brief for designers all the harder, of course, but personally, that’s the kind of challenge I’d relish.

#9142. New Eames Museum in California Funded in Part by Trump Appointee

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

A new museum devoted to design legends Charles and Ray Eames in the Bay Area of Northern California received more than $25 million in initial funding from Joe Gebbia, an Airbnb cofounder who is currently a Tesla board member and previously worked with Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), according to a report by SFGATE.

#9141. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#9140. Page\Park uses local stone and timber for school wellbeing hub in Edinburgh

Scottish architecture studio Page\Park has completed The Allardice Centre, a health and wellbeing hub for Fettes College in Edinburgh, which is topped with a lantern-like roof.

Named after the independent day and boarding school’s alumnus David Allardice, the 469-square-metre centre brings together medical and pastoral care services in a fully accessible building nestled into a wooded plot.

According to Page\Park, the centre’s design was informed by the late Allardice’s interest in Eastern philosophy, in particular the elemental philosophy of Wuxing, which led to a palette of timber, stone and metal.

The building’s structure is made from Scots-grown timber, while Darney stone quarried nearby forms the external load-bearing cladding, which is contrasted by a bronze roof.

“Allardice spent much of his working life in East Asia, and was drawn to ancient Chinese philosophy and the five essential elements, fire, water, wood, metal and earth,” the studio told Dezeen.

“This narrative directly influenced the design, materiality and construction approach, which can be seen through the strata-like stone cladding, burnt bronze metal roof, and connection to the outside,” it added.

The Allardice Centre is organised across a single storey, with an open wellbeing hub at its centre, wrapped by a series of individual treatment and counselling rooms overlooking the surrounding woodland.

Illuminating the central hub is a mono-pitched, lantern-like roof. This creates a ring of clerestory windows, framed by the exposed glued-laminated timber (glulam) structure designed in collaboration with Scottish engineering firm Will Rudd.

“Fitting the full brief for both medical and pastoral functions into this constrained site, while avoiding level changes to maximise accessibility, forced the plan to be quite deep,” explained the studio.

“Bringing natural light into this deep plan therefore became a challenge. To resolve this, the glulam structure extends and branches out at high level to reveal a triple-glazed clerestory lantern formed of timber curtain walling,” it added.

Inside The Allardice Centre, white walls allow the timber structure to come to the fore. In the treatment rooms, leaf-print and green fabrics create a visual connection to the surrounding site, which was developed by landscape architects Harrison Stevens.

“We were interested in the didactic implications of exposing the glulam timber frame, offering an insight into how the building was crafted, celebrating its sustainability principles and the elemental philosophy underpinning the design,” said the studio.

“The Darney stone chosen for the project was quarried only 75 kilometres away, and had fantastic mineral veins through it which paired neatly with the varying course sizes, leaning into the earth element theme, and giving a sense of permanence,” it added.

Other projects in Edinburgh recently featured on Dezeen include the extension of a Georgian townhouse by Pend, which complemented the existing stone structure with skinny red brickwork.

Elsewhere, Page\Park recently completed a teaching building for the University of Stirling, which was shortlisted for the 2025 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award.

#9139. Cosmic Leonora Carrington Painting Reemerges at Auction After 70 Years

In a dreamy development for the fall auction season, another Surrealist standout has resurfaced on the market. After seven decades out of public view, Leonora Carrington’s Fil d’Or (1953) will appear at Heritage Auctions in New York on November 10, with an estimate of $250,000–$350,000.

Its title translates from the French to “gold thread,” a term traditionally referring to the delicate metal wire used to ornament luxury textiles. The cosmic bird Carrington depicts appears to be composed of intersecting threads, all emanating from a single source: the golden galaxy pulsing in place of a heart. Related Articles Lehmann Maupin and Gallery Wendi Norris to Collaborate on Two-Part Exhibition Pairing Leonora Carrington and Cecilia Vicuña Almine Rech Announces Collaboration with the Consejo Leonora Carrington and rossogranada

She employed a technique developed by her former partner, the artist Max Ernst, known as grattage, in which layers of fresh paint are scraped with a blade or spatula. The process exposes unexpected shapes and patterns through texture, creating an impression of spontaneous motion, as though the picture were realizing itself.

“By choosing this title, Leonora Carrington shifts focus away from the obvious. Instead, she redirects the viewer’s awareness to consider coexisting, alternative meanings—in this case, her meaning—by experimenting with how we emotionally respond to different thoughts,” Heritage Auctions wrote in its citation. “Ultimately, Fil d’Or demonstrates that words hold multiple meanings, explores how others perceive them, and questions whether they are truly understood at all.”

Carrington created Fil d’Or in Mexico, to which she fled after the outbreak of World War II in Europe. There, she formed a swift friendship with fellow refugees, including the Surrealist painter Remedios Varos and photographer Kati Horna, over alchemy, the occult, and esoteric symbolism.

Carrington died in Mexico City in 2011, at the age of 94. Although she achieved success in her lifetime as both a visual artist and a writer, female Surrealists have experienced an unprecedented surge in market interest over the past decade, thanks in part to Cecilia Alemani’s 2022 Venice Biennale, titled after Carrington’s book The Milk of Dreams. The market reached a high point in 2024, when Carrington’s 1945 painting Les Distractions de Dagobert sold for $28.5 million at Sotheby’s, setting an auction record for the artist. The sale easily surpassed her previous auction record of $3.2 million, set in 2022.

Recently, I’ve written for Creative Bloq's sister site Digital Camera World about a run of photographic rediscoveries. For instance, F Holland Day’s 1898 series The Seven Words resurfaced in September. Then in October, we saw a newly found cache of photos that document the making of the 1926 horror film Faust. These antiquated forms of physical media sat untouched for a century or more, and yet remain totally viewable. Amazing, really.

Now, let's do a thought experiment. If you're old enough, picture the digital work you made 20 years ago. That might be a website design, assets for a CD-ROM, a vector illustration… whatever.

Ask yourself: could you locate and open those files today? If you’re anything like me, the honest answer is “mostly no”.

It's ironic, really. Because digital work has no tangible physical presence, we tend to think of it as eternal. In truth, though, it's kind of the opposite.

This March, I visited memory card manufacturer Lexar’s facilities in Shenzhen, China. And one moment there has stuck with me ever since.

In a press conference, the company's representative explained that the flash memory used in consumer memory cards and SSDs can start losing data within a year if you leave them in a drawer and don't power them up.

Lexar told me it’s developing a dedicated device to address this issue, but it's early days. In contrast, a print just sits there, being a print.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Meanwhile, if you're putting your work online, there's more bad news. A Pew Research Center study found that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were no longer accessible a decade later. Platforms are no safer. Back in 2019, MySpace admitted that a server migration had wiped photos, videos and music uploaded between 2003 and 2015: an estimated 50 million songs from 14 million artists.

Its advice to users was to keep their own backups. But wherever you back stuff up, basically, you're running the same risk. As the sudden closure of Sora highlighted, venture capitalists don't really care about protecting your stuff as much as you do.

There's also the problem of actually opening files in years to come. Built something in Flash in 2012? I doubt you'll be able to salvage it now, after Adobe shuttered the format in 2020, and that's just one example among many.

So what can we do? There are few basic rules we all should be following if we want to be able to access our work in 2030, 2040 and further ahead. The first is to follow the 3-2-1 rule. Keep three copies of anything important, on two different types of storage, with one stored offsite or in the cloud. It's not a foolproof method, but it does reduce the odds of losing stuff exponentially.

Secondly, every few months or so, power up your SSDs and memory cards, so firmware can do its job. Thirdly, export your final files to open formats like TIFF, PNG, SVG or PDF/A, which are more likely to be readable in decades to come.

Fourthly, treat platforms as shop windows, not storerooms. And finally, print your work. As long as you can avoid floods or fires, paper-based storage has a better track record than digital.

Is this seems a bit of a faff, I'd have to agree. But consider this. If future historians end up knowing more about 1926 than 2026, it won’t be for lack of material. It’ll be because we couldn't be bothered to look after it – and what will future generations think of us then?

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9137. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#9135. Pace CEO Marc Glimcher Responds to Reports of Financial Losses, Says Gallery Will Open New Location in Europe

Pace Gallery’s CEO Marc Glimcher is looking ahead and washing over the headlines over the last week regarding the gallery’s financial accounts.

“We’re all off the bottom, we just had a record art fair at Art Basel Paris, and we’ve had sellout shows of primarily young artists—everything is turning,” he told ARTnews in a phone interview on Monday, noting that the business is already back in the black and will open a new location in Europe “fairly soon.”

Pace Gallery has been shifting its real estate portfolio recently. Back in June, Pace’s London property was put on the market, with the gallery saying it was seeking a “less corporate” space in the British capital, while in September, Pace announced it was seeking tenants for part of its Chelsea headquarters. Glimcher reiterated that London remains a “great market.” He added, “London is working very well. We are never going to close in London.” Related Articles Pace Reports $5.6 M. Loss for International Business, With Glimchers Pledging to Keep It Afloat Pace Gallery Reports Losses of 35.5 Percent for 2024 With 'Real Change' Underway

He said that many galleries use the city as an international hub where “a lot of work gets done managing Asian and European units. It’s a great place to have headquarters and it carries a lot of weight the way New York does.”

Glimcher hinted that he already has “a couple of amazing choices” for Pace’s next London property, The gallery is currently situated on Hanover Square, taking up 8,600 square feet. The gallery will be “about the same size, and we’re going to a more prime location that fits the model we’ve been working on,” said Glimcher, contending that the business has “done a lot of internal reengineering of the way the companies work together” and that the success of its arms in Berlin and Japan have been “very instructive” to the overall strategy of the business.

Pace Gallery published its 2024 accounts last week with Companies House, the British government’s business register. The filing was 10 months late and recorded a turnover of $67.7 million in 2024, a 35.5 percent drop from 2023, which cashed in $105 million. A pre-tax loss of $2,429 was recorded for 2024 compared to a $6.8 million profit for 2023. (The mega-gallery’s UK registered company, The Pace Gallery Limited, serves as the umbrella company for its operations in Europe and Asia, excluding Tokyo as well as the US.)

Shortly after that, Pace Gallery’s 2025 accounts were published, with turnover dipping 2.6 percent to $65.9 million. “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently,” said Glimcher. “We’re in a process of keeping those units a little more autonomous and self-sufficient, to do that, you have to shift the balance sheet.”

In June, the gallery laid off 50 staffers and dropped 50 artists from its roster, including Keith Coventry, TeamLab, John Gerrard, and Glenn Kaino. (Pace now represents a total of 85 artists.) But now that the dust has settled, Glimcher said the gallery is ready for new life.

“We’re always adding artists and the artists that left the roster were artists [who] we were really not working with,” he said. “There were areas that we were really not engaged with, it wasn’t benefiting them or us. They were not artists that we had a super active engagement with. It’s just about focusing your efforts to do less better than doing more not as well.”

Glimcher said that all galleries have been making changes of late and—at least, for Pace—new strategies are starting topaying off.

“We have had an extremely profitable year already in Los Angeles. The things we’ve done are already bearing fruit, and they’re bearing fruit because the market has substantially changed,” he said. “What we’re doing in London, when we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody.”

From the first ever touchscreen on Mac to the super bright and colourful 'PROLED' XDR display, there are quite a few candidates for the headline feature of Apple's new MacBook Pro. But judging by the reaction in the room during the launch in LA last week, the most popular addition might not be that new at all.

Readers of a certain vintage will remember the illuminated Apple logo. The light-up fruit used to adorn every Apple laptop, and was a (somewhat distracting) mainstay of cafes, trains and DJ performances. In 2015, Apple unceremoniously killed the illuminated logo, replacing it with a mirrored version. But as of last week, it's back – and it seems people are happy about it.

Now, the cynical among you might think the reason for the addition is to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display stand out as new in public. There's always something to differentiate a new Apple product from the previous generation, even if it's simply new colours. But from a distance, this new MacBook Pro looks almost identical to non PROLED models. How are we supposed to quietly show it off in a cafe? With the 'new' illuminated logo, of course!

But the less cynical among you might see this as yet another sign that under new CEO John Ternus, Apple is rediscovering its sense of fun. From the brand's wild new TikTok presence to the colourful (and cheap) MacBook Neo, Apple seems to be stepping outside of its space grey prison and embracing a sense of friendliness we haven't seen for years. And it's going down well.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.
