Why distance-based pricing changes the domestic flying equation

Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

#9132. ARTnews and Hublot Host Dinner at New York Headquarters of Kid Super

On Wednesday night, ARTnews and Hublot hosted a dinner at the New York headquarters of artist and fashion designer Kid Super (Colm Dillane).

Guests included collector Carla Shen; Frank Suznjevic, president of Hublot Americas; ARTnews and Art in America editor-in-chief Sarah Douglas; Time to Drive festival founder Perri Dash; fashion designer Mobolaji Dawodu; collector Viljon Caka; Gazelli Art House senior director Haley Shaw; filmmaker Saam Farahmand; collector and commentator Jeff Magid; gallerist Adam Cohen; artist Jonathan Gardenhire; Brooklyn Museum trustee Carla Shen; curator Anwarii Musa, and real estate developer Ben Levine. Related Articles Pace CEO Marc Glimcher Responds to Reports of Financial Losses, Says Gallery Will Open New Location in Europe Cosmic Leonora Carrington Painting Reemerges at Auction After 70 Years

PJ Monte of Monte’s Fine Foods, also known as the Sauce Boss, provided dinner.

In a conversation with Douglas, Dillane said he had first found the art world somewhat inaccessible, and he compared his entrée into it to the reception he got early on in fashion. “I was really an outsider [there] as well,” he said. “I got rejected three times from the official calendar [at Paris Fashion Week]…. [T]hey finally said yes. Once I broke into fashion, I realized that behind this wall there’s really interesting people who care about new ideas.”

Dillane gave attendees a tour of his 10,000-square-foot headquarters. The building includes a Hublot-sponsored rooftop soccer pitch, an art studio, a podcast studio, a store, and other spaces for all kinds of creative work. “When everyone got here, I couldn’t wait to tour them around the building,” Dillane told the guests. “This is my greatest work, and I think it encapsulates [my] whole practice.” Of the many creative avenues he has pursued, he said, “For me, all of these different mediums were pushing towards the same spirit…. There’s a mischievousness to it…. There’s bringing people together. I want to capture the feeling that I feel when I’m in New York, where anything feels possible.”

#9131. Norman Foster creates first-ever watch in collaboration with Lebond

British architect Norman Foster has unveiled his first watch, designed with watch brand Lebond in a process he said was “very similar to architecture.”

The mechanical watch has a sleek silhouette with an integrated strap. According to Foster, the design process began with a reevaluation of what we assume a watch should look like.

“We wanted to look again at something very familiar and reconsider it as a complete object, with the case, the strap, the dial and the movement all part of a system,” Foster told Dezeen.

“Normally, you have a watch case and then you attach a strap to it. We started to question the obvious. Why should they feel like two separate objects? Once we began thinking of the strap as a continuation of the case, the whole watch started to come together.”

As a result, the Lebond Norman Foster has a 38.5-millimetre-wide Grade 5 titanium case that widens to 40 millimetres where it connects to the integrated strap, creating a streamlined design.

The architect also got rid of the traditional watch lugs, wrapping the strap around the timepiece’s titanium case instead.

“Removing the conventional lugs gave us the continuous profile, but it also made the watch more comfortable and more integrated,” Foster explained.

The Lebond Norman Foster, with its distinctive rotor, also evokes aviation design – a reference to Foster’s interest in flying, as well as to his history of international travel.

This comes across in a very practical way, with the watch’s bidirectional rotating 12-hour bezel allowing the wearer to read a second time zone using the main hour hand.

Its dial is protected by a domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating, and the watch is water-resistant to 50 metres.

It is currently available in two versions: the Natural Titanium Edition, which has a micro-sandblasted titanium case, a brushed-metal dial and a grey rubber strap, and the Black Edition, which features a matte black DLC-coated titanium case matched with a black lacquered dial and hands and a black rubber strap.

Foster designed the watch to allow people to customise it, swapping cases and straps at will, and more versions will be released over time.

“A watch is intensely personal. You wear it, you travel with it and it becomes part of your everyday life,” Foster said. “This led to the potential for a wide range of colour combinations and the ability to customise the watch”

“By designing an easy attachment mechanism, the user is able to interchange elements and create personal versions,” he continued.

“I proposed a watch that could move naturally between very different situations, working in the studio, being on a building site, travelling or going somewhere formal. It should not feel precious or limited to one particular setting.”

This marks the first time that Foster, who is known as the most successful architect in history, has designed a watch, but he didn’t find the process daunting.

“I have never really thought that scale changes the nature of design,” Foster said. “Whether it is a city, a building, a chair or a watch, you are still asking the same questions: how does it work, how is it made, and how do all the parts come together?”

“The process is also very similar to architecture,” he continued.

“It becomes one of refinement, sketches, prototypes, adjustments and then more adjustments. You explore options to finally arrive at the essential idea and then you keep refining it until everything seems inevitable.”

Last year, in celebration of Foster’s 90th birthday, we looked at twelve defining projects from his long career. Next month, the architect will give the keynote speech at the Dezeen Awards party.

#9130. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

A year ago, a lot of people couldn't quite believe it when Canva made Affinity free. Suddenly, the three paid-for apps obtained through the acquisition of Serif were rolled into a single piece of creative software covering everything from photo editing to vector art and desktop publishing, simultaneously serving as a free Photoshop alternative, InDesign alt and Illustrator alt.

There had to be a catch, and one of the suspicions was that the new Affinity would be unlikely to get regular upgrades or improvements. One year on, Canva seems to be defying those predictions. It added new raw photo editing capabilities last month, with more colour, sharpening and detail adjustments. Today, it's completed things by adding one major element that was still missing for many creatives' workflows: a dedicated Affinity for iPad.

The individual Affinity apps (Affinity Photo 2, Designer 2, Publisher 2) were previously available for iPad before last year's launch of the unified free Affinity for desktop. Users who had bought them could continue using the apps, but they didn't support the new .af file format.

The new single-app Affinity for iPad brings the bulk of the combined desktop software to Apple tablets but designed specifically for a touch-first interface. It also takes advantage of Apple Pencil capabilities like pressure and tilt for sketching or for masking images, as well as Apple Pencil Pro's barrel roll, squeeze and hover features.

The app features Sketch Studio for freehand drawing and sketch-to-vector workflows, and several iPad-first features like a Mask Tool and Sketch to Shapes.

Like on the desktop app, Affinity for iPad uses the same .af file format across sketch, vector, photo and layout processes to make cross-media workflows easier. Non-destructive edits render in real time and there's no need for assets to be exported, converted or remade.

For sketching, there's a brush library with controls to shape each brush, while sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again. The iPad app also includes Affinity's raw image editing capabilities and the ability to create print-ready multi-page documents.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

AI tools, including Generative Expand, upscaling, denoising, and Decompose Layer to split a flat image into editable layers, are available with a subscription via Canva AI Studio.

An increasing range of major software is now available in the form of dedicated iPad apps, from Adobe's main apps like Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere to DaVinci Resolve for video editing and Maxon's ZBrush for 3D sculpting. This means the powerful iPad Pro can now be used to its full potential for creative work, allowing more mobile workflows, either for working remotely or simply allowing creatives to take time away from the desk to work in another place before coming back to pick things up on desktop.

#9128. Pace’s Marc Glimcher Responds to Reported Financial Loss, High Museum of Art Former COO Sentenced to Prison for Embezzlement, and More: Morning Links for November 3, 2026

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

KEEP UP THE PACE. Pace CEO Marc Glimcher responded to ARTnews about reports of financial losses and the gallery’s direction. “Everything is turning,” Glimcher said over the phone, noting a “record” Art Basel Paris last month, “sellout shows” helping business get back in the black and a new location expansion in Europe coming “fairly soon.” Last week, Pace published its accounts with Companies House, showing significant losses in turnover for 2024 and 2025. Glimcher said: “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently.” He added that the 50 artists dropped by the gallery in June “were not artists that we had a super active engagement with,” and “it wasn’t benefiting them or us.” He is also working on moving into a new space in London, to be decided. “When we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody,” he said. DOING TIME. The High Museum of Art’s former COO, Brady Lum, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison, followed by one year of supervised release, for embezzling over $600,000 from the museum by tampering with invoices and approving personal purchases, announced Georgia’s United States Attorney’s Office. “Lum brazenly pilfered hundreds of thousands of dollars from a beloved civic institution to pay for his high-end guitars and other personal items,” said US Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “His appalling breach of trust damaged not only the High Museum but also the larger art community,” he added. Lum served as Atlanta’s High Museum of Art COO from January 2, 2019, to December 9, 2025. He has paid back the full, stolen $607,688 to the museum, plus another $500,000 to cover costs the museum spent to uncover his own crime.

Lawmakers in Italy are examining a new bill to create a committee that will research provenance and facilitate the restitution of art and cultural items pillaged by Nazis and Italian police between 1933 and 1945. [The Art Newspaper]

A city council in New South Wales will not exhibit Phil Buehler’s “Wall of Tears” installation memorializing the names of children killed in Gaza, due to cited safety concerns. [The Guardian]

In an interview pegged to a new limited-edition collaboration with watchmaker Hublot, Jeff Koons said: “I never think about price. I know I’m associated with very valuable things, but it’s not something I think about. I believe in the value that things have for humanity, in a conceptual way. In the knowledge and care they reflect.” [El País]

Despite turmoil at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, its prestigious annual Kennedy Center Honors celebration for lifetime achievement is pressing forward, awarding the likes of pop singer Paul Anka, playwright David Mamet, actor Andy Garcia, and country singer Barbara Mandrell. [The New York Times]

An unknown, intimate drawing by Duncan Grant of Vanessa Bell, the English artist and sister of Virginia Woolf, was discovered amid research for Tate Britain’s forthcoming show on Bell and Grant. [FAD Magazine]

ART WANTED, DEAD OR ALIVE. Thanks to an inventive “WANTED” campaignby the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans in France, aimed at tracking down hundreds of WWII-era looted artworks, one painting has just been found, reports Le Journal des Arts. The stolen painting by Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster, titled Le Buveur, was located at an auction house in Switzerland and is expected to be restituted to the museum shortly. Its owner purchased the painting in the 1990s, agreed to hand over the artwork, and said they had not known of its problematic provenance. In June 1940, Nazis attacked the city of Orléans, burning an annex of its fine arts museum, known as the Musée Paul Fourché, which was subsequently almost entirely ransacked, likely by people on both sides of the conflict. Some 350 paintings from Europe, dating back to the 16th century, were lost.

#9127. KPF completes Texas's tallest skyscraper in Austin

Photography by Jason O'Rear (unless otherwise stated)

New York architecture studio KPF has completed Waterline in Austin, Texas, a supertall skyscraper with a mixed-use programme that slopes away from Lady Bird Lake as it rises. It has a form that resembles a “cowboy boot”, according to its designers.

KPF, which is known for its skyscrapers around the world, was not originally meant to design the 1,025-foot-tall (312-metre-tall) structure.

The building’s original developer was the coworking real estate company WeWork, which selected a design by its collaborator, architecture studio BIG, through a competition.

However, after WeWork’s failed IPO in 2019 and governance scandals, KPF was brought back in to take up the mantle on the project, which had already begun its early construction.

KPF president James von Klemperer told Dezeen that the concept of a “we-building” or a mixed-use building with overlapping functions remained part of the DNA of the building as the project was awarded to KPF by its new development team.

“Space isn’t as proprietary,” said von Klemperer of the project and concept. “No, it weaves together with other things, and with the spaces that are shared at the rooftop of the base of the building.”

The structure features hotel and office programmes at the bottom, with luxury residences at the top. Double-height exterior floorplates supported by massive columns mark changes in the programme from the exterior, and the whole building slopes up and away from Lady Bird Lake, a wide section of the Colorado River that flows through Austin.

Deference to the waterway was one of the main goals of the project, as were nods to the regional heritage, and a desire not to “strangle” the low-lying historic Rainey District to the southeast of the site.

It was originally supposed to be multiple towers, but the studio decided that shoring its density into a single tower allowed for these goals to be achieved.

“The project grew into the design, if you will, the way it inclines down like a cowboy boot at the base,” said von Klemperer

“It inflects towards Lady Bird Lake, and I think that was a powerful profile in everybody’s estimation, because it says something about a vertical structure becoming a piece of landscape or geology.”

Von Klemperer also contrasted the skyscraper, with its wide-grid facade and columns, with black-glass skyscrapers with wide bodies that block urban view corridors, referencing recent skyscraper construction in New York.

It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community.

“It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community,” he said, adding that Waterline’s facade, which features rust-coloured details to reference Texas geology, is “lacy” and full of moments “where your eye can see through or see some depth or see pattern”.

“We hoped to make a beautiful little piece of waterway facade.”

Working closely with landscape architecture studio TBG Partners, the structure steps up from the creek, with massive columns meeting the ground plane.

These columns form what von Klemperer compared to an amphitheatre of sorts, adding “urban drama”.

“Cities should have places that support urban drama, and I think already this has shown it really works,” he said.

At the centre of the structure’s stepped podium is a paseo from the city to the water that is lined with stone and makes the lower part of the structure, mostly retail and parking, more porous.

On top of the podium, amenity spaces serve the 1 Hotel, which is taking over the middle part of the programme.

The columns at the base and at the breaks were designed with oak trees in mind.

The studio included some V-shaped columns to add to this character, but also to structurally aid the building as the floorplates changed to accommodate the programme shifts.

“From an office grid to the residential grid, those misalignments along the perimeter were actually beneficial for getting a better column placement in the residential above,” said KPF design director Andrew Klare.

At the top of the building is a sky lounge, and the bulkhead has a slight angle that echoes the slope of the skyscraper.

Von Klemperer said both the shifts in the facade and the tilted top of the skyscraper were subtle nods to the city’s slogan – Keep Austin Weird.

“It’s not an exceedingly weird gesture that interrupts the skyline, but it’s a bit of whimsy, which is in character with the rest of the skyscraper’s geometries,” he said. “It destabilises the conventional grid of the world.”

The mixed-use programme also came to pass during the Covid-19 pandemic, which was a period of doubt in the feasibility of downtown cores.

This didn’t stop the project, but intensified the studio’s desire to create an open building with multiple uses and to “multiply” the uses of the podium.

“It restores your faith in the urban agenda of development – to make such a mixed-use project with levels of shared use throughout,” said von Klemperer.

Other recent skyscrapers by KPF include a “beaux-arts” supertall in New York that is nearing completion and a pair of skyscrapers in Istanbul.

#9126. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

It's been a while since I saw an optical illusion good enough to share, but I couldn't resist this one, which is like a combination of two of our favourite ever optical illusions. I present: the spinning horse meets the blue and black or white and gold dress – and it's baffling the internet.

This is a real life video of a horse standing in a stable. And the horse is clearly black... except, it isn't. Apparently it's white. I absolutely cannot see this however many times I come back to it, but people in the comments have learned how the horse is actually in shadow, clicked off and back onto it, and then can see that it's white.

I'll share it below – can you see the horse as its real colour, or are you stuck in the same camp as me?

With 4,500 upvotes on Reddit, the r/opticalillusions subreddit is taken with this illusion.

"I can no longer see it as a black horse but at first it was as black as midnight. Now it's white and I cant make it go back," one amazed comment reads.

"It's the exact same effect as the White/Gold Blue/Black dress," explains another. "It's an image where the subject is in shadow but the background is in bright sunlight and our brain struggles to differentiate the two lighting conditions."

Other comments share tips on how to achieve the effect if you're struggling.

#9124. C Next Designers EMEA brings together over 250 professionals for design conference in Almería

For the ninth edition of the C Next Designers design conference, Spanish brand Cosentino brought together designers from Europe, Africa and the Middle East for three days of talks focused on “design as a driver of change”.

The event was held from 13 to 16 October in venues across Almería, Spain and included talks by designers such as Ron Arad, Karim Rashid and design studio Studiopepe.

It is the fourth iteration of the event held in Spain and the ninth worldwide.

This year’s conference focused on the theme Design to Transform, which champions “design as a force capable of reshaping society and adding value to it”, according to the team.

The first day opened with a welcome at the Cabo Gata Beach Hotel.

On Wednesday, the event moved to Cosentino’s industrial park in Cantoria, where Cosentino CEO Pilar Cosentino gave opening remarks.

Architect and designer Ron Arad then spoke with Cosentino commercial director for Europe, Jorge Lope about his career and collaborations with the brand, before the day ended with a guided tour of Cosentino’s facilities, including a local natural stone warehouse.

The day also featured the presentation of the latest product innovations by Valentín Tijeras, global vice president of product.

The second day took place at the Almería Science and Technology Park (PITA) and included presentations by brands Novara, Jung, Speho, TECE and Gaggenau.

Karim Rashid and Studiopepe then gave keynote speeches, which were a highlight of the day.

Dezeen editorial director (special projects) Max Fraser also moderated two panels as part of the event.

The first, held with Dornbracht, focused on hyper-personalisation as a creative tool and featured C’est Ici Design founder Monica Arango, founder of Black Architecture Danko Lekic and head of global channel management at Dornbracht Sascha Bialoian.

The second panel examined how design is changing our everyday habits, and featured Fran Silvestre Arquitectos founder Fran Silvestre, ZHA associate director Bidisha Sinha and founder of AS Architect Ayşin Sevgi Karakurt Macit.

Studio Haus closed the panels, and the event concluded with a gala dinner in the Cloister of Almería Cathedral, which was informed by the Dekton Artik Nodes collection, a new Cosentino material.

Cosentino previously launched Nara, a beige-toned porcelain surface designed to celebrate natural stone and Éclos, which was designed to be free of crystalline silica.

Last year’s C Next Designers conference featured talks by Sabine Marcelis and Peter Ippolito or Nini Andrade Silva.

Concept artist Christian Forsgren explains how Arrowhead takes hardware from Blender blockout to in-engine testing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the Scope of Authority Warbond bringing new sniper rifles, ghillie armour, and mine grenades to Helldivers 2, we asked Arrowhead concept artist Christian Forsgren how that kind of hardware goes from Blender blockout to an in-game weapon. The answer is speed. “I can see how it actually handles in a player’s hands straight away, not weeks later,” he says. For weapons and machinery, that matters: a badly judged few centimetres can be the difference between convincing military hardware and something from a toy shop.

Each asset starts with a brief and a team brainstorm. Forsgren then builds a rough 3D blockout in Blender, refines the functionality, materials and finish, and pushes it into Arrowhead’s Stingray engine to see how it behaves in real time.

That loop helps give Helldivers 2 its battered, believable look. Weapons have to be mechanically plausible, and procedural materials add edge wear, grime and volumetric detail “without ever doing a single second of UVs”. Forsgren has also built a Blender pipeline for the game’s Warbond banners, producing renders at a higher fidelity than the game itself can manage, in the series’ propaganda-poster style.

There’s plenty here for Blender users beyond games, too: the scripts and add-ons Forsgren uses to speed up his work, the custom tools Arrowhead uses to move assets between Blender and the engine, and why the studio lets artists build their own workflows. The takeaway is that the best pipeline helps artists make better decisions, faster, with fewer hand-offs.

For more on Helldivers 2, visit Arrowhead Game Studios.

Christian Forsgren: It starts with a brief, then it’s team brainstorming. After that team brainstorm I take over and focus on ideas we have landed on and take it to a point where we can start to iterate. Say I'm building a weapon: I take the agreed upon brief and build the concept model in Blender, sometimes I do simple sketches depending on the asset to bounce around the team but most of the time it's straight into Blender for easy blockouts to help with scale and animation approximations. When that has reached a reasonable state I take it further and focus on functionality, materials, and how we want the finished asset to look like.

When that is greenlit Blender's job ends once the asset's ready to live in the game. We push it straight into Stingray, the game engine, and we're play-testing it in real time so I can see how it actually handles in a player's hands straight away, not weeks later. That's where Stingray takes over: real lighting, real scale, how it sits next to everything else. Then it's a loop with coders, designers, 3D artists and animators until it actually fits the game, not just looks good on its own.

CF: My own setup runs on scripts I've built and collected over time. Everything from camera related addons that help me manage the compositor, HDRI’s, Lights, focal length and Depth of field. Addons that help me create procedural materials in the shader editor. Pie menus to help me speed up access to all different kinds of Blender nested menus. The asset library is an insanely helpful addition to Blender to help me keep track of textures, materials, assets, animations and have them always available without opening a file explorer. The ecosystem's incredible and most problems I hit, someone's already solved it.

At a studio level, Arrowhead's built custom exporters and importers to bridge Blender and our engine. The problem we were solving was speed and consistency. Without that bridge, every asset needs manual rebuilding or re-checking every time it crosses from Blender into the engine, and that adds up fast across a whole team.

CF: Military realism drives a lot of it. Every weapon, like the arm-mounted cannons on our Exosuits (the mech suits players pilot in Helldivers 2), has to be functionally plausible, with every part sized to actually fit how it works mechanically. That attention to real, physical logic is a big part of why it reads as lived-in rather than designed.

Blender's procedural tools do a lot of heavy lifting too. I can generate complex backgrounds like planets and star systems without hand-painting any of it, and Cycles with some simple HDRIs gets me high-quality results without a huge amount of manual tweaking. That procedural system is always handy when it comes to the nitty-gritty textures as well; I can get there very fast with the procedural texturing tools inside Blender. All the nodes available to me make it a breeze to create edge wear, grungy textures and interesting volumetrics without ever doing a single second of UV’s.

For the war bond banners specifically, I built a proper Blender pipeline to replace what used to just be in-game screenshots with simple text put on top; now it has grown to larger marketing material where the most important part of the image is made in Blender in conjunction with studio tools to get in-game assets into Blender to be rendered at higher fidelity than we could ever achieve in-game to really row home that gritty propaganda feel we always strive for.

CF: Because we can export an asset into Stingray and see it working within a few hours, we iterate fast, and the feedback loop with coders, designers and animators continues until the design fits the game.

All games go through late asset iterations, it may be because what we initially thought was something fitting of the fantasy has changed because other assets in the game brought this particular one into the wrong direction so now the concept has to change.

Since Helldivers is such a vast world we often find other uses for assets that maybe not made the cut so we try to salvage things at later stages or for different themes just so interesting ideas don’t get lost but since we built the workflow to use 3D early and iterate on blockouts early it rarely happens.

CF: Blender is my all-in-one package for modelling, animation, texturing,simulation and rendering, so I don't have to jump between programs, which is why I prefer it to other 3D packages which are more specific in their use cases. Blender is also the most user friendly, working with other packages was always way too daunting as a concept

artist, but there was something in the way Blender did everything I wanted in the same package that made it a go to choice.

CF: Arrowhead gives us creative freedom to choose our own tools and workflows but we have some specific ones everyone uses to bridge the game engine and Blender. A lot of the 3D artists at the studio have very different setups based on how they like to work, which I think is really important. Pushing everyone to use the same exact

setup can have some advantages, but giving team members the tools to customise Blender how they like to is what keeps that individuality.

The studio-specific tools are there to get finished work from Blender into the engine, not to dictate how that work is made. Everyone has their own setup when it comes to the tools they like to work with, be it specific add-ons if you are an environment artist or if you are a hard surface artist or character artist. All these use vastly different workflows, so empowering them to use what they think is best is super important, and it also helps create an environment where different disciplines can empower each other.

CF: Honestly, it's being able to push early concept blockouts straight from Blender into the engine and have it working almost immediately. I didn't expect that to become as central as it has. It's changed how fast we can actually iterate, because I'm not waiting around to see if something works now we can test animations, scale and overall look within the engine in the blink of an eye.

CF: What transfers, I think, is the mindset more than any specific tool. We lean on Blender because it's open source and shows what you can do without breaking the bank, whether you're a studio or working completely solo, it gives you real, tangible results rather than something generated for you. Having modelling, texturing and animation all in one place matters most if you're working alone and don't want to juggle five different programs.

The other thing that transfers is freedom in your own process. Arrowhead gives artists a lot of freedom in which tools and workflows they use, and everyone on the team works a bit differently. On my end, that shows up in small ways. Procedural tools save a lot of time by generating things like backgrounds automatically instead of building them by hand, and I do colour and exposure work right inside the render with the Photographer add-on instead of switching to Photoshop.

CF: The industry is always changing, so it is very hard to be on top of what works and what doesn’t. But with the knowledge and connections I possess today, I could more easily create workflows that would be in line with how I can work more closely with the rest of the teams. How can we bridge the gap between artists, animators and designers? For example, it’s an everlasting process of building pipelines, so who knows what is on the horizon.

#9122. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9121. Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room

Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital.

Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings.

Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather.

The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition, and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing.

The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces.

Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture.

“Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.”

Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine.

“The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said.

The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom, who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project, the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas.

Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future.

For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space.

In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold.

The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions.

Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut.

Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving.

Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

#9120. matteo thun transforms 72 apartments inside milan’s iconic brutalist torre velasca

working within the protected 1958 tower, the studio pairs original architectural details with velvet walls and italian design classics.

Matteo Thun & Partners has unveiled the interiors of 72 residences inside Milan’s Torre Velasca, the postwar skyscraper designed by Italian architecture studio BBPR. The project occupies floors 19 through 26, and introduces suites and apartments for short- and long-term stays. This includes duplex penthouses overlooking the city. Set to open in phases beginning in fall 2026, the renovated interiors bring rich colors and Italian design classics into one of Milan’s most iconic buildings.

Completed in 1958, Torre Velasca was designed by BBPR on a site heavily damaged during World War II. Its unusual silhouette, with a broad residential volume projecting above a narrower office tower, takes inspiration from medieval Lombard architecture, especially the Filarete Tower at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco. Angled reinforced-concrete supports carry the upper floors, giving the building its distinctive mushroom-like profile. Even after the design stirred considerable debate among modernist architects at the time, it’s since become an unmistakable part of Milan’s skyline.

The new interiors follow an extensive restoration of Torre Velasca led by Milan-based studio Asti Architetti for developer Hines, completed in 2025. For the team at Matteo Thun & Partners, working within the protected building meant accommodating much of its original architecture. Tiles in the kitchens and bathrooms have been preserved, along with historic doors and window frames. The apartments also retain their original loggias, which punctuate the tower’s upper volume and frame vast views across Milan.

The existing proportions presented their own challenges. Ceilings are relatively low, and many of the rooms are compact, prompting the studio to introduce glossy finishes that reflect daylight and give the interiors a greater sense of space. Floor plans have been adjusted to accommodate larger showers and walk-in closets.

Working with Italy’s Ministry of Culture, the architects were also able to partially remove a kitchen wall, introducing a cocktail counter that connects the cooking and living areas. The opening allows natural light to reach further into the kitchen while creating a casual setting for gathering.

The material palette draws directly from Torre Velasca’s architecture. Working with Italian textile house Dedar, Matteo Thun & Partners developed custom velvet wall coverings in a dusty pink inspired by the building’s exterior plaster.

The color brings some of the tower’s character indoors, where it is paired with mustard-yellow sofas custom-designed for Molteni and coffee tables with distinctive stone finishes. Warm wood and deep green accents complete the interiors, giving the rooms a character that feels connected to Milan’s long history of furniture design.

An ecclectic collection of furnishings draw on several decades of Italian design, with pieces by Gio Ponti alongside work by Afra and Tobia Scarpa. Cassina’s Utrecht armchair appears in blue felt with contrasting green stitching, while lighting by Oluce has been produced in colors selected specifically for the apartments. Matteo Thun & Partners has also designed custom wardrobes and bedside furniture, manufactured by Italian producers.

Beyond the apartments, Matteo Thun & Partners has designed the reception and lobby spaces, as well as corridors toward the rear of the ground floor. The residences form part of a wider redevelopment that preserves Torre Velasca’s mixed-use character, with offices continuing to occupy the lower floors and hospitality spaces introduced throughout the building. The upper residences, operated as part of METT Milan Torre Velasca, extend this layout with accommodation for both shorter visits and longer stays.

From the street, Torre Velasca’s immense concrete brackets appear to support an entire block of apartments above the city. Inside, the rooms are surprisingly modest in scale. Their low ceilings and deep window openings are reminders of the building’s original design, even among the new furnishings. It is this contrast between the monumental exterior and the domestic spaces within that gives the project its particular character, allowing one of Milan’s most recognizable architectural landmarks to be experienced from the inside.

the apartments offer sweeping views across Milan, including the nearby Duomoa richly patterned counter introduces an informal gathering space beside the kitchen

It's time for the world of high quality wired earphones (or IEMs) to get excited, as it's the annual 11/11 sales period, and there are some awesome discounts on already well-priced products.

This year, I want to focus on six of my favourite IEM deals from HiFiGo – one of the biggest operators in the space. These are all earphones that I've actually tried and tested myself, and that I feel hit the sweet spot of excellent sound quality, build quality and value for money.

My absolute favourite would be the Juzear Light Shuttle, which I reviewed only last month. It is my 'neutral with bass-boost' release of the year, and it's currently down from $190 to $155 over at AliExpress.

All six of these IEMs are featured either on my list of the best budget IEMs currently on the market, or my pick of the best IEM under $500.

This is the last IEM that I reviewed, and I was really impressed by its warm/neutral sound, with a textured bass response and clear, clean, yet not over the top treble. Plenty to like about this one, especially its new price of $121.

This is the cheapest IEM on the list, and it's a really good buy. Made of all-metal shells, it's more durable than most $40 IEMs out there, and its take on a V-shape sound signature is fun and energetic. A good all-rounder, though things do get a little spicy up in the treble some times.

This 8-driver IEM is the most expensive IEM on the list, but it's also my favourite. It does musical with smooth upper mids like few other IEMs that I've heard, and there's a fairly big bass shelf in there too for fun. This is smooth and exact, and $251 is an absolute bargain down from $389. Read my Aful Performer 8S review for more.

This two dynamic driver and four balanced armature hybrid IEM is a bit of a classic – and for good reason. It's one of the first to popularise the 'neutral with bass boost' sound signature, otherwise known as New Meta. That means its well balanced in the mids, but has the excitement of elevated bass. One of the best IEMs on the list.

I haven't reviewed the 1900 yet, but I was impressed with its bright/clear sound. It reminded me of its more expensive brother the Binary EP321 – but $100 cheaper. At $157 I think this is another super strong option for the HiFiGo sale.

The MiracleOne is the most recent IEM that I've received, and there's lots of like. The comfort is S tier, and that goes a long way when you've got a crowd-pleasing sound to back it up. Honestly I think this single DD isn't the best option at its retail price of $200, but at $155 it becomes a compelling option.

#9118. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#9117. Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea "without traditional thresholds"

Architecture studio Büro Ole Scheeren has revealed designs for the Suseong Continuum, a snaking, concrete art gallery in Daegu, South Korea.

Set to be built within the city’s Yeonhwaji park, the 364-square-metre gallery was designed specifically for showcasing digital art.

Berlin-based Büro Ole Scheeren designed the gallery as a continuous space, without any enclosed rooms and or doorways, in a bid to reflect the “flows” of digital art.

“We wanted to build a gallery without traditional thresholds: a gradient of realities that morph into one another as you gradually move through the space,” studio founder Ole Scheeren said.

“The substance of digital art is not rooted in the physical domain of distinct objects and isolated experiences… it exists in a world of overlaps and connections, where one condition potentially flows into the next.”

“Landscape, circulation and exhibition become a continuous experience,” the studio added.

The Suseong Continuum gallery was unveiled as part of this year’s Suseong International Biennale, which invites architects to realise permanent public works across Daegu.

Commissioned by the Suseong District Government, the design by Büro Ole Scheeren is expected to open for the biennale’s 2028 edition.

Once complete, visitors will access the space via a winding path, from which the gallery was designed to emerge as an extrusion.

Conceived as a “continuation of the landscape”, the gallery’s twisting volume will be partially embedded into the park’s topography and oriented toward a nearby lotus pond.

Its structure will be built using board-marked concrete to create a rough exterior texture. Inside, this textured surface will transition to smooth concrete walls for projecting media onto.

According to Büro Ole Scheeren, the gallery’s layout and materiality were designed to reflect the transition from the park’s natural landscape to the digital interiors.

“Technology is often seen as an opposite to nature,” Scheeren said. “With Suseong Continuum we wanted to explore how we can create a way of extending the way we perceive the relationship between both domains – a journey that starts in the park and that seamlessly carries you into the digital realm.”

“There is no single moment where one world ends and the other begins, it is a continuous transformation.”

“What begins as natural landscape gradually transforms into digital media,” the studio added.

Renders of the gallery’s stripped-back interior reveal its immersive exhibition spaces framed by curving walls.

A layered ceiling will run the building’s full length to conceal all lighting and technical infrastructure, which was developed by the studio in collaboration with the Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe.

“The interior unfolds as a spatial gradient in which light, sound, enclosure and immersion shift gradually along the visitor’s route,” the studio said.

“Curving walls widen into open spaces and tighten into passages; atmospheres transform rather than switch,” it added.

The design will remain on show at the Suseong International Biennale until 22 November.

In Shenzhen, China, the studio has revealed plans for skyscrapers with “waterfall” facades and its design for the Róng Museum of Arts is currently under construction.

Nintendo developers reveal the challenges of getting the art style and gameplay right.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first tease of the The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake divided opinion with its revelation of what looked to be a highly realistic art style for one of Nintendo's most loved adventures. However, many fears will have been assuaged by the Zelda Ocarina of Time previews.

While the game is much more than a fresh coat of paint for the 1998 classic, with new controls, richer environments, extra dialogue, voiced cutscenes and fixes for some of the creakier bits of the original, it's also clear that Nintendo has been faithful to the original in many ways. Some of the thinking behind that comes across in a new series of interviews with developers. They reveal the vision for retaining a stylised look to the game's art, and confess that certain changes were considered but ruled out because they interfered with the core structure of the game.

As we noted in our preview, the new Hyrule of the Ocarina of Time remake remains very faithful to the shapes and colours of the N64 original but rebuilds them with sumptuous lighting and far more detail, from the grain in the wood and foliage to the stitching on Link’s tunic.

Despite the Nintendo Switch 2's far superior graphics capabilities compared to the N64, art director Aya Shida emphasises that the goal wasn't merely to make the classic look as realistic as possible. In early in development, the team used phrases like “a puppet-show feel” and “the analog feel of practical effects films” as concepts to aim for.

"We wanted to rebuild Hyrule as a rich, dense world that felt as though it could truly exist, while retaining the feel of the original. At the same time, we wanted its colorful and quirky characters to feel like a natural part of that world. Figuring out how to strike the right balance became one of the main themes of the art development," she says in Nintendo's Ask the Developer series.

"Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Aya adds.

The team began by drawing sketches of Link, Zelda and the other characters and creating a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree. Although the N64 designs and the new ones look very different due to the exaggerated features in the former, Aya says the aim was to preserve familiarity, which included paying particular consideration to how characters look from a distance "so that players would feel they were still the same characters they remembered, even after 28 years".

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

A lot of attention also went into the textures of the characters’ clothing. While they're much more detailed, they couldn't be took perfect. For example, the young Link's clothes needed to look handmade to be believable.

"We started by asking what kind of fabric those children might actually weave and wear," Aya reveals. "We looked at materials in museums and even experimented with making our own fabric from thread to get a better sense of what it should be like. For this game, the hardware allowed us to depict that level of detail, but that also meant we needed to do our research until we had a clear idea of what we wanted to create. As a design team, we often talked about imagining the story behind every object in the game as we created it."

While the objective was always to be faithful to the original game's focus on the joy of exploration, The Legend of Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma reveals that the Ocarina of Time remake could have ended up with warp points like in Breath of the Wild.

"In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry. I thought we needed to address this in this new version," he said.

However, developers discovered that adding the warp points to Ocarina of Time eliminated an important part of the game: the moments of discovery.

"Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again," he says.

One gameplay change that did make it into the remake is the addition of a dedicated jump button for Link, whereas he hopped automatically off certain ledges in the original. This will take some getting used to, especially mid-fight, but should be a welcome change for fiddly moments.

Eiji also commented on the reason for remaking Ocarina of Time in the first place as the franchise approached its 40th anniversary. He says that a significant part of the motivation was to ensure that the team working on the Zelda series today truly understands the original game's significance to the series as a whole.

"By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development," he suggests.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on 5 November, 2026.

You can read the full interviews with developers on the Nintendo website.

#9115. Montana acquires sustainable furniture maker Takt

Montana has announced its buyout of fellow Danish design brand Takt, known for its solid wood furniture and pioneering approach to sustainable design.

Founded in 2019 by trained physicist and former Lego and Bang & Olufsen executive Henrik Taudorf Lorensen, Takt makes modern Scandinavian furniture from FSC-certified wood that is low-carbon, flat-pack and designed for disassembly.

Its future launches and existing catalogue, including products such as the Cross chair by British design duo Pearson Lloyd and Anderssen & Voll’s Spoke sofa, will now be sold under the collection name Takt by Montana.

Montana CEO Joakim Lassen said he hopes they will act as an understated counterpart to Montana’s existing selection of colourful modular furniture – including the Montana System storage – and bring valuable learnings about sustainability to the table.

“Takt brings experience with materials and the environment, and we are looking forward to bringing our respective experience together and taking this work even further,” he said.

Takt is known for its ambitious approach to sustainability, focused on driving down emissions primarily through the design of its products rather than operational cuts, to become net zero by 2030.

The company assesses the carbon footprint of its products throughout their entire lifecycle using the EU’s Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) single score, in a bid to bring down its emissions, and claims to be the only design brand to consistently have all of its products marked with the EU Ecolabel.

“I have a background as a scientist, so it was important to me to start measuring things,” Lorensen told Dezeen during our Carbon Revolution series. “The starting point was to get a grasp of the impact of the choices we’re making.”

Lorensen will join Montana Furniture’s board, sharing his experience and perspective on sustainability, while Takt employees will be integrated into Montana’s organisation “as far as possible”, the company said.

By gaining access to the established, international infrastructure of Montana, which has been operating since 1982, Lorensen hopes that Takt’s furniture will be able to reach a larger audience.

“The past few years have been an exciting and instructive journey for TAKT,” he said. “We have built a brand where materials and the environment have been central, and we have collaborated with a number of talented and celebrated designers. “

“Now it is time for TAKT’s next chapter, and we are delighted that it will be written together with Montana.”
